title: SpaceX wins FCC approval to deploy 1 million orbital data center satellites
summary: SpaceX won approval from the FCC to put 1 million orbital data center satellites into space, a proposal that was opposed by Amazon and other groups.
body: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk 's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday. Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI. Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." The FCC, in its authorization filing , noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC ( Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)." In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan." The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims." The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr , who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone. Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher , which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October. In March, Jeff Bezos ' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January. Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday. "Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense." The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."

title: Nvidia leads tech sell-off as Huang comeback rally fizzles and AI concerns return
summary: Nvidia and other AI-linked stocks fell as investors weighed AI spending, inflation and higher-rate risks.
body: Technology stocks fell on Wednesday as excitement over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's return faded and failed to calm concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite declined 0.6% and traded off its lows, recovering from steeper losses earlier in the session. Semiconductor stocks dragged on the index, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF that tracks the sector edged down 1%. "We just feel that this is panic right now," Venu Krishna, head of U.S. equity strategy at Barclays, told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday. "What the market is telling you is that the AI growth narrative has hit a wall and given the centrality of that theme at the economic level, the market is expecting some sort of a macro shock," he added. After notching one of its best days on record Monday, Nvidia has fallen in the days since and slumped 4% Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices , Marvell Technology and Intel all edged lower. Micron Technology declined 4%. Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday briefly revived appetite for tech stocks but didn't fully calm investor concerns over the high costs tied to the AI build-out and worries of a potential slowdown. Other stocks tied to the AI trade also plummeted. Oracle fell more than 5%. CoreWeave and Nebius moved lower. AI lab Anthropic bucked the sell-off, however, and climbed more than 4% after shares dropped below last week's blockbuster IPO price. Wednesday's declines also came as Wall Street digested a hot inflation reading that fueled concerns that higher interest rates could dent demand for growth stocks, including tech. Amazon and Alphabet each declined about 2%. Microsoft and Tesla lost more than 1% and Meta traded 3% higher.

title: There are 5,100 newly minted Anthropic millionaires—here’s all the stuff they don’t tell you about when you suddenly get rich
summary: Anthropic’s IPO made about 5,100 employees paper millionaires. Experts explain the risks of sudden wealth.
body: Things are about to get very weird for the thousands of employees of Anthropic who just became, or soon will become, multimillionaires. Anthropic's IPO on Nov. 19 turned around 5,100 nonfounder "Ants," as the company's staffers are known, into "paper millionaires," and at least 400 will be worth north of $100 million. Few of us will ever make a million-dollar windfall from an employer. And fewer still will win the lottery or magically land a massive sum from an estranged rich uncle. But don't be too jealous of these employees' gains. Sure, money can buy a lot — and it would be hard to say no if you do strike it rich — but there are a remarkable number of downsides to sudden wealth. And they may explain why you likely won't see all of Anthropic's newly minted millionaire employees heading for the exits. First of all, these new moguls won't be able to access all their wealth immediately. The terms of the stock sale outlined in Anthropic's revised S-1 allow employees to cash out up to 10% of the value of their holdings on the first day of trading following the date of the prospectus, but the rest can only be exercised after various vesting periods pass or lock-up terms are achieved, based on the individual's agreements with the company. Some won't be able to realize all their gains for years. There are many financial institutions willing to lend based on paper gains, or to buy options — but their wealth will also continue to fluctuate with the rise and fall of the company's stock price. Even after those riches become liquid, research shows that only a small but still significant percentage of employees will leave as a direct result of their new wealth. No, they aren't jetting off to the South Pacific to board their new yacht — which is what I would do in my "I just got $10 million" fantasy. Instead, according to a 2017 study from the Federal Reserve , an estimated 17.5% of employees at a newly public company will use their newfound wealth as a financial cushion to join another pre-IPO startup or form another company. These departures, the study finds, may be particularly painful for Anthropic since the most valuable and entrepreneurially minded employees tend to bolt for this reason. Experts who deal with suddenly wealthy employees expect that many will keep on working because they love it. "They're successful people in their own right," said David Rust, a financial advisor and co-founder of wealth management firm Quartz Financial in Austin, Texas. Rust said that of his firm's high-tech employee clients who get sudden IPO wealth, "very few just go play golf every day. They want to stay busy and active, and a lot of them will scale back depending on their age, but very few of them say, 'OK, I'm done with that.'" Others will keep working because their payout wasn't life-changing, said Susan Bradley, a certified financial planner and founder of The Sudden Money Institute, a Palm Beach Gardens, Florida-based financial advisory firm that specializes in clients undergoing sudden wealth events. That's especially true for those whose millions measure in the low single digits. "You can go through $2 million pretty quickly in the world we live in," said Bradley. A sum north of $1 million might seem life-changing to most of America, but it's chump change in Anthropic's headquarters city of San Francisco, the fifth most expensive city in the United States, with nearby San Jose coming in at third, according to a Q3 2026 Cost of Living report from Council on Community and Economic Research, which tracks metro- and state-level economic data. In 2025, the Bay Area had the second-highest number of people with a net worth of $100 million or more of any major metro in the world, according to a study by New World Wealth, a market research firm, in conjunction with Henley & Partners, a global residency and citizenship planning firm. title: Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly to buy Lukoil's oil and gas assets outside Russia, sources say
summary: The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said.
body: Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly's asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil's assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC. The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said. The deal transfers Lukoil's international refineries and other production assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the U.S.-led group, the sources said. It also includes retail gas stations in the U.S., Europe and Asia, they said. The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control is expected to sign off on the deal but final approval is still needed, the sources said. The deal would give the U.S.-led group about 350,000 barrels per day of production. The agreement would allow Europe to buy fuel such as diesel previously produced by Lukoil through the U.S.-led group rather than Russia.

title: Kalshi traders say the odds of states imposing data center moratoriums is more likely than not
summary: After Democrats swept Congress and key governor races, Kalshi traders lowered the odds that at least four states would pause data center build-out this year.
body: On Wednesday morning, Kalshi traders put the probability above 55% that at least four states would adopt data center moratoriums this year. After Democrats swept Congress and key governor races during the midterm elections, Kalshi traders put the odds that at least four states would pause data center construction at about 75%. Since Nov. 22, the probability that at least four states would adopt moratoriums rose again, to 57% from 52%. The contract asks "How many states will adopt data center moratoriums this year?" and will be verified from state governments. On July 14, New York became the first state to impose a one-year pause on certain state permits for hyperscale data centers. Various local governments have also ordered moratoriums on data centers this year. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., called for a national data center moratorium the day after the midterms on social media , signaling growing pushback against the build-out. Meanwhile, some investors say unease surrounding the artificial intelligence trade is partly an emotional or sentiment-driven reaction. Doug Clinton, founder and CEO of Intelligent Alpha, told CNBC's " Closing Bell: Overtime " the AI sell-off is psychological. "I actually think it is difficult to point to some fundamental data point from here that all of a sudden would make investors okay," Clinton said. AI-related stocks slumped again Wednesday. Nvidia and Oracle slid more than 8%, while Anthropic tumbled 6% and Alphabet slid 5.5%. On Friday, the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average entered corrections, down 10% from their recent highs, while the Nasdaq Composite declined more than 5% following Anthropic's blockbuster public offering the day before. body: The S&P 500 was down as much as 3.2%, and the Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 4% in the morning. Anthropic and Meta were among the first to turn, and the buying spread through the afternoon. By the close, the S&P 500 was down just 0.25%, the Nasdaq Composite was off 0.62%, and the Russell 2000 was up 0.71%. The small-cap gain showed how far the recovery had spread, even with chip stocks still weighing on the Nasdaq. The USD was strongest against the Australian dollar, with AUDUSD down 0.15% to 0.6628, and weakest against the Swiss franc, with USDCHF down 0.56% to 0.8309. USDCAD fell 0.36% to 1.4215 as oil rebounded. EURUSD edged up to 1.0973, GBPUSD was little changed at 1.3114, USDJPY slipped to 159.19, and NZDUSD rose to 0.5486. The longer end led the decline. The move was consistent with demand for Treasuries during the equity selloff, even as the PCE report showed annual core inflation picking up. At the session lows, the S&P 500 was down about 231 points, or 3.2%, and the Nasdaq Composite was down roughly 1,090 points, or 4.6%. Buyers stepped in during the afternoon, and by the close those losses had narrowed to 18 points and 148 points, respectively. The Russell 2000 turned positive and finished up 0.71% as the rebound broadened. Nvidia was down nearly 9% in the morning, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was off more than 7%. Micron bounced about 9% from its low during the afternoon recovery and was still down on the day at that point. Anthropic traded as low as $73.85, well below its $83 IPO price, before rebounding. Two sessions after Jensen Huang’s return sparked a relief rally, investors are still asking how much profit all that AI spending will generate and how long it will take. images.investinglive.com Europe closed with the Nasdaq 100 still down nearly 4%. Spain and Italy led the losses. investinglive.com Core inflation picked up as real spending stalled. October core PCE rose 0.3% on the month, as expected. body: U.S.-Backed Consortium Signs Deal for Lukoil's International Oil Empire What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… Crude oil prices are down this week, extending a losing streak prompted by predictions of a supply glut. The ones doing the predictions are citing the rebound in export flows out of the Persian Gulf, but they seem to be forgetting something. These export flows were up in September and October. Now, they’re down. The war is not over, and neither is the risk to global oil supply. One recent indication of that was the news that Chinese refiners, state-owned and independent, have ramped up their buying from abroad—and not only from the Middle East. Sinopec, for instance, has bought about 20 million barrels of crude since the start of this month from West Africa alone, for delivery next month. That is equivalent to all Chinese refiners’ West African oil purchases in a typical month. Yet purchases from the Middle East are also on the rise, the report, by Bloomberg, said, suggesting export rates are indeed normalizing. Except the number of tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz has gone significantly higher as well. Just at the beginning of this week, three tankers were damaged after they struck mines, although the UK Maritime Trade Operations said three vessels were struck by unidentified projectiles. Mines and/or attacks on tankers have become a daily occurrence in the chokepoint—and daily traffic rates are down. Related: Iraq Refuses to Accept OPEC+ Assessment of its Production Capacity Indeed, tanker traffic in Hormuz was already down in early October, from the September rebound. That was according to Kpler, which has turned into the go-to source of tanker traffic information for all major outlets. It was Kpler analysts who said that by October 8, the number of tankers traversing the Strait of Hormuz had fallen to the lowest in two months, meaning July, to some 10.1 million barrels daily. “That is back to its September average, but 74% of its pre-war level,” the analysts noted at the time. This does not exactly match the glut story that some investment banks and the International Energy Agency are putting forward, and that has depressed prices and quite likely lulled oil traders into a false sense of security that all is back to normal in the Persian Gulf and a formal peace is only a matter of time—even as President Trump suggested to Fox News that the United States could restart its attacks on Iranian targets in 2027. Meanwhile, Kpler has reported that after hitting a wartime high of over 20 million barrels daily in mid-October, tanker traffic in Hormuz began to decline, first to 16.03 million barrels daily towards the end of the month, falling further to 15.77 million barrels daily for the first week of November, and further still to 13.96 million barrels daily for the second week of the current month. Reuters’ Clyde Russell cited Kpler’s numbers in his latest column, noting that since the start of November, attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf had reached 12 so far, after a total of 17 recorded for October. “It seems more than just a coincidence that export volumes from the Middle East are trending lower as attacks on vessels are trending higher,” Russell noted. It is, indeed, quite hard to see these developments as a coincidence, but it is interesting that oil traders appear to be ignoring the latest data, instead hanging on to the assumption that the September rebound was irreversible and the global oil market is about to tip into oversupply. This is a risky assumption because, as suggested by President Trump, the war is not over. There is no ceasefire. Just because there are no reports of bombs raining on Iran and its Gulf neighbors, it does not mean things cannot change, often rather abruptly, as we have seen earlier this year. body: U.S.-Backed Consortium Signs Deal for Lukoil's International Oil Empire US billionaire Todd Boehly has signed a deal with Lukoil to buy the sanctioned Russian oil company's international assets through a share swap backed by the US International Development Finance Corp (DFC), Reuters reported on Wednesday. The consortium will exchange Lukoil securities worth $10 billion for the assets. The securities were bought from US and British funds and from US depositary banks that held them for retail investors, according to a person familiar with the terms. Western investors' Lukoil shares were frozen after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 and written down. "We're basically exchanging shares that are worthless to Americans ... for cash that is going back to them," said Boehly, chief executive of the asset manager Eldridge. The shares will be held in escrow in the UAE rather than going to Lukoil, the person said, to win approval from the Treasury Department, which has barred any windfall to the Russian company. Two people familiar with the terms valued the portfolio at about $16 billion. It covers operations in 11 countries producing around 350,000 barrels per day, including oilfields in Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan, refineries in the Netherlands, Bulgaria and Romania, and a network of service stations that includes some in the United States. In early November, Reuters reported that the assets were initially valued at $22 billion. Through the DFC, the US government will receive a share of future profits once the private investors recoup their capital and an agreed return, and it will have a role on the company's board. "Moving strategic energy infrastructure assets into US or allied partners' hands is a key policy priority of the administration," a DFC official said. The deal needs approval from the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), and Boehly said closing could take up to a year. The consortium now includes US bank Xtellus Partners and UAE-based Catena Investment Holding. Two partners left last week: the Syrian-Qatari Al-Khayyat brothers and Abu Dhabi's International Holding Company. Washington sanctioned Lukoil in October 2025, which forced the company to sell its foreign holdings. Two earlier buyers failed to close. Gunvor withdrew its offer after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called the trader the "Kremlin's puppet." Lukoil then agreed in January to sell the assets to Carlyle , excluding its stakes in Kazakhstan's Karachaganak and Tengizchevroil projects and the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, but OFAC never licensed that deal. OFAC has now issued 12 versions of its license for the sale talks. The latest , issued November 19, allows negotiations to continue until December 19. body: U.S.-Backed Consortium Signs Deal for Lukoil's International Oil Empire Kazakhstan has joined Iraq in asking OPEC+ to raise its estimate of the country's crude production capacity, Reuters reported Wednesday , citing people familiar with the matter. The request comes four days before the group meets to set its output policy for 2027. The review is OPEC's first, and will assess how much oil each member can produce sustainably, and its findings will help set production targets for next year. One of the sources told Reuters that OPEC+ is holding talks this week with the members that dispute their assessments. US consultancy DeGolyer and MacNaughton is assessing capacity for every OPEC+ member except Russia, Iran and Venezuela. Kazakhstan's energy ministry confirmed the review had taken place but did not comment on its findings or next steps. Kazakhstan's OPEC+ quota for November and December is 1.628 million barrels per day, according to OPEC data . The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated Kazakh crude output at 1.76 million bpd in October, about 8% above that target. Chevron began production from the $48 billion Future Growth Project at Kazakhstan's Tengiz field in January 2025. Export disruptions have also capped Kazakh output this year. The Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), which carries more than 80% of Kazakhstan's oil exports to a terminal near Novorossiysk on Russia's Black Sea coast, suspended loadings in July after drone strikes on tankers at the terminal. Kazakh oil and condensate output fell about 21% to 1.63 million bpd from a July average of 2.07 million bpd, and production at Tengiz fell 56%. In March, the energy ministry had already cut its 2026 production plan to 96–98 million tonnes from 100.5 million tonnes, citing attacks on the CPC and the situation at Tengiz. Iraq disputes a preliminary finding that puts its capacity at 4.9 million bpd. Baghdad has a quota of 4.431 million bpd and wants OPEC+ to recognize around 6 million bpd of capacity. The IEA puts Iraq's sustainable capacity at 4.87 million bpd. Iraq has warned it may leave OPEC if its quota is not raised, according to Reuters. The challenges follow the UAE’s exit from OPEC and OPEC+ on May 1. Abu Dhabi had argued for years that its quota did not account for its investment in new capacity. Angola left OPEC in January 2024. Middle East OPEC+ members have pumped below their quotas for much of 2026 because the Iran war disrupted Gulf flows. Traders are concerned a surplus could build in the rest of 2026 and in 2027 as those flows recover, which has weighed on oil prices. body: U.S.-Backed Consortium Signs Deal for Lukoil's International Oil Empire Oil prices climbed on Wednesday after Yemen's Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, the kingdom's largest, and Saudi Arabia said it had shot down four drones over the site. As of 10:16 a.m. ET, Brent crude traded at $93.60 per barrel, up $2.20 or 2.41%, and West Texas Intermediate traded at $83.51, up $1.46 or 1.78%. Saudi-led coalition spokesman Turki Al-Maliki said air defenses destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura on Wednesday morning, and that fragments fell from the interceptions with no injuries in an initial assessment. The coalition did not say the refinery had been hit. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the strike was "accurate and direct" and had caused fires at the site, and claimed a separate attack on the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh. NASA satellite imagery reviewed by Reuters showed thick black smoke around the refinery, covering about 600 square kilometers. Saudi Aramco and the Saudi government did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment. The Ras Tanura refinery processes 550,000 barrels per day, about 16% of Saudi refining capacity, according to The National. The adjacent terminal can load about 6.5 million bpd of crude and was Saudi Arabia's main export outlet until Yanbu took on more volume during the Iran war. Loadings at Ras Tanura resumed in late June after a halt of about four months that followed a March 2 drone attack. Wednesday's claim follows two days of escalation. On Tuesday, a strike on the Riyadh tower that houses the Public Investment Fund injured 11 people, and the coalition blamed the Houthis. Saree warned the same day that "Jeddah port and all Saudi enemy ports on the Red Sea coast will be targets" if the coalition bombed Hodeidah. The coalition then struck Hodeidah port along with targets in Saada and Amran. As of early Wednesday, maritime security firm Vanguard Tech had recorded no attacks on Saudi ports. The Houthis have claimed repeated strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure this autumn. They claimed a ballistic missile attack on Ras Tanura on October 27, and three days later claimed strikes on the Ras Tanura and Rabigh refineries and Aramco's Abqaiq facility. An attack on November 9 set fire to the East-West pipeline, which carries crude to Yanbu. PVM oil analyst Tamas Varga told Reuters that the Houthi statement set off Wednesday's rally by raising the geopolitical risk premium, and that traders covering short positions before the US Thanksgiving holiday could add to the gains. Zhenqiang Seto of LSEG said uncertainty over OPEC+ policy for 2027 before Sunday's meeting was also lifting prices. title: Gold at $8,000 could signal dollar crisis: economist
summary: Alasdair Macleod warns that the Federal Reserve may have to sacrifice the currency’s purchasing power to protect markets.
body: Alasdair Macleod warns that the Federal Reserve may have to sacrifice the currency’s purchasing power to protect markets. Gold’s next rally could expose a sharp deterioration in the value of the US dollar, economist and financial commentator Alasdair Macleod says. Despite uncertainty over the timing of a rebound amid expectations of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike, Macleod sees the precious metal potentially reaching $8,000 per oz. within six months. “It doesn’t mean that gold has gone up,” Macleod told MINING.COM host Devan Murugan on the latest Top of Mine episode. “It means the dollar has gone down. And this is the point which I think everybody misses.” Macleod’s outlook challenges conventional investment thinking, particularly the tendency to view gold through the lens of interest rates rather than as a means of preserving wealth against currency depreciation. For him, investors need to better understand gold and what it means to hold it. “We live in this Keynesian world where the first reaction is you sell gold for whatever reason, like ‘rising interest rates is bad for gold because of the opportunity cost,’ or all this rubbish which actually just completely misunderstands what gold is,” he said. Macleod sees that the problem is in the American market, where investors own little gold while we are on the verge of an ‘uncomfortable’ bear market in equities. A liquidity squeeze, he argues, could prompt indiscriminate asset selling. “The basic message I have for everyone is the risk is in credit,” Macleod said. “Get out of credit, get into physical gold and be happy.” Macleod said that he wouldn’t want to be in the Fed’s position, as that choice to raise interest rates will decide what is protected: either the dollar or the financial system. “They will do whatever it takes to try and rescue the economy and rescue financial markets,” he said. “That becomes a priority, not protecting the dollar.” Central bank intervention to ease liquidity pressures could come at the expense of confidence in the currency, Macleod warns. “It’s their currency going down. And when people generally realize that, particularly the users of the currency, then the currency is finished.”

title: Harmony Gold bets on copper as South African mines age

body: Australian operations could yield 100,000 tonnes annually by 2029, with a major Papua New Guinea project offering upside. Harmony Gold Mining (JSE: HAR)(NYSE: HMY), South Africa’s largest gold producer by volume, is banking on its expansion into Australasia to protect long-term profitability as output declines and costs rise at its ageing domestic mines. The company’s CSA mine and Eva Copper development in Australia could produce a combined 100,000 tonnes of copper annually by 2029, chief executive officer Beyers Nel told MINING.COM in an interview. The Wafi-Golpu copper-gold project in Papua New Guinea, which Harmony jointly owns with Newmont (NYSE: NEM), could further bolster production once the partners secure permits. “If you think about South Africa, we are a bit out of runway on new gold mining assets,” Nel said. “There are maybe one or two assets left in South Africa that are good quality, but they are not necessarily for sale.” Harmony remains among the few gold producers generating profits from South Africa’s deep and costly underground mines. Larger rivals AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE:AU)(JSE: ANG) and Gold Fields (NYSE, JSE:GFI) have long pursued growth elsewhere in Africa, Australia and the Americas as South Africa’s once-fabled gold deposits become increasingly depleted of commercially viable ore. Harmony expects to produce 1.3 million to 1.4 million oz. of gold in fiscal 2027 after output fell 3.4% to 1.43 million oz. in the year through June 2026. Mining at greater depths and rising operating costs threaten to erode earnings from its traditional revenue base. While Harmony isn’t actively pursuing acquisitions, it could target Australian mines transitioning to underground operations, where its deep-level mining expertise could give it a competitive advantage. That strategy underpinned its $1 billion acquisition of CSA, currently its only producing copper mine. “We would look for value from that perspective, something that someone might not want to do,” Nel said. Harmony still sees opportunities to extract additional value from its South African operations. The company has been mining higher-than-expected grades at Mponeng, the world’s deepest gold mine, although Nel acknowledged the richer ore won’t last indefinitely. The miner is studying opportunities to recover more gold from surface tailings and extend the life of its Hidden Valley mine in Papua New Guinea. Together, those initiatives could add 250,000 oz. annually and help sustain group production above 1.5 million ounces. Advances in robotics and mining technology could also eventually allow Harmony to safely extend Mponeng beyond the depths envisaged in its current mine plan, Nel said. Harmony expects CSA to produce 28,000 to 30,000 tonnes of copper in fiscal 2027 before ramping up to 40,000 tonnes annually within three years. It plans to spend $1.55 billion to $1.75 billion developing Eva Copper, targeting annual production of about 60,000 tonnes by around 2029. The Australasian assets could account for 30% of group production by 2036, up from about 16% currently, Nel said. Investors, however, remain cautious about the company’s ability to deliver on its targets. “I don’t think we get any value for the copper assets in the share price,” Nel said. title: Copper price sinks to 2026 low as mining stocks brace for further losses
summary: In every copper bear market since 1970, prices gave back the vast majority of the bull market's gains, a new analysis shows.
body: In every copper bear market since 1970, prices gave back the vast majority of the bull market's gains, a new analysis shows. Copper fell to its lowest level this year on Wednesday, extending a selloff that has erased about $145 billion from the market value of the world’s biggest copper miners in November. Comex copper for December delivery fell 2.1% to $5.25 a pound ($11,584 a tonne) around midday in New York, after touching $5.222. That is below the March 20 settlement of $5.3425, the previous low for 2026, and a settlement at today’s level would be the lowest since early December last year. The red metal is now down 7% this year and almost 19% in November, and sits 24% below its record settlement of $6.889 on September 9. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange fell 1.9% to $11,596 a tonne in afternoon trading in London, its weakest since December 16. New York and London prices are now roughly level, after tariff bets kept Comex at a hefty premium for most of the past two years. History offers little comfort to copper bulls. Every bear market in copper since 1970 “has taken back the vast majority of each bull market’s gains,” John Gross wrote in The Copper Journal on Friday. He calls it the “Give Back”. In each of the 11 bull markets before this one, a 10% fall from the peak was followed by a 20% drop and a bear market, Gross found. Losses from the high ranged from 32% to 69% and averaged 49%. Comex copper crossed his 20% line, $5.44 a pound on his measure, this week. A 49% loss from September’s record would take Comex copper to about $3.50 a pound. Gross does not forecast the outcome of this cycle, and his study looks only at price behaviour, setting aside fundamentals and economics. Stocks have a better record: after a 10% fall, the S&P 500 has gone on to break through its 20% line only about half the time, he noted. New US tariffs and inflation data added to the pressure on Wednesday. The Trump administration proposed duties on 14 trading partners , including 20% on China, and figures released the same morning showed US inflation rose further in October, stoking worries about more interest rate hikes. Nvidia fell more than 8%, the Nasdaq Composite 3.5% and the S&P 500 2.4%. Copper itself is largely outside the new package. For 13 of the 14 economies, the proposed duties would not apply to goods already covered by Section 232 tariffs, including copper articles, according to law firm Baker McKenzie . The decision that matters most for the metal, a proposed 15% tariff on refined copper imports from 2027, remains unresolved . BMO Capital Markets expects the selloff to run until Washington signals its tariff intentions or prices fall far enough to hit supply, potentially in the $10,000 to $11,000 a tonne range, the bank said this week . Financial flows have overpowered a physical market where visible exchange stocks cover only about two days of consumption, BMO said, and traders have booked an estimated 30,000 to 100,000 tonnes of US copper for shipment to China, a sign they are losing faith in a tariff that would keep US stockpiles sealed off. The bank stands by its structurally bullish medium-term view. “People had been trying to get into the hard-assets trade and AI expansion and growth, but I think this unwrapping and unwinding has more to go,” George Griffiths, head of markets at AMT Futures, told Reuters. Open interest in copper has declined significantly, he said. title: Nine dead, 17 trapped after illegal gold mine floods in Indonesia
summary: Rescue crews pump water from a 100-metre shaft in West Java as difficult terrain and poor visibility hamper efforts.
body: Rescue crews pump water from a 100-metre shaft in West Java as difficult terrain and poor visibility hamper efforts. Rescue crews pumping water from flooded shaft. ( Image: Screenshot from Global News Network+ | YouTube. ) Indonesian rescuers are searching for miners trapped underground after heavy rains inundated an unauthorized gold mining operation in West Java province. The miners have been trapped since Monday in a 100-metre-deep shaft in the Pongkor area of Bogor, a mountainous region 60 km south of Jakarta. Authorities have been pumping water from the shaft to facilitate recovery efforts, the search and rescue agency said Wednesday. “The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely,” Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said according to local news outlet Detik . The disaster underscores the challenges Indonesia faces in regulating small-scale mining across its resource-rich but often remote regions, where informal operations provide precarious livelihoods for thousands of workers. State-owned miner Antam, which operates gold mines in Pongkor, said the incident occurred at an unauthorized site unrelated to its operations. “The problem was that nobody reported it and nobody wanted to report it because the activity was illegal,” said Muhammad Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor disaster mitigation agency. The incident comes after authorities shut down about 30 gold mining pits in a separate area of Bogor last week. Workers at informal mining operations face persistent threats from landslides and tunnel collapses. Gold ore processing also frequently involves highly toxic substances such as mercury and cyanide, with miners often using little or no personal protective equipment.

title: ValOre seeks financing for $135M Brazil gold deal
summary: Água Azul would give ValOre a second Brazilian property, as well as a first operating asset.
body: Água Azul would give ValOre a second Brazilian property, as well as a first operating asset. View of ValOre's Pedra Branca property in Brazil. Credit: ValOre Metals. Canadian developer ValOre Metals (TSXV: VO; US-OTC: KVLQF) agreed to buy the Água Azul gold mine in Brazil for $135 million (C$193 million) — more than 20 times the company’s market value before trading was halted Tuesday. Vancouver-based ValOre plans to buy Bemisa Água Azul Mineração and an associated landholding entity from the Opportunity Holding investment fund, according to a statement Tuesday. The agreement will require a $90 million payment at closing, followed by $20 million after one year and $25 million after two years, subject to adjustments. ValOre, which still needs to secure acquisition funding, expects the deal to close by Jan. 15, subject to TSX Venture Exchange acceptance. “Advanced” financing discussions covering the purchase, working capital and initial development spending are ongoing, the company said. Under the agreement, ValOre has a one-time option within four months of closing to settle all $45 million of deferred payments for $30 million, subject to United States inflation adjustments. Exercising it would cut the nominal purchase price to $120 million. Located about 1,900 km northwest of Sao Paulo, Água Azul would give ValOre a second Brazilian property, as well as a first operating asset. The company is already developing the Pedra Branca platinum group elements project in Ceará state, about 200 km from Fortaleza. Água Azul includes a 206-sq.-km land package that hosts the Abelhas, Juliano and Campos Altos deposit areas along a 15-km structural trend. Its Abelhas open-pit gold mine feeds a plant processing about 120,000 tonnes of material a year. A preliminary economic assessment dated July 28 evaluates increasing the plant’s processing capacity to 2.85 million tonnes a year, following a three-year development period. The study estimates $297 million in initial capital, including plant expansion, pre-stripping and contingency. At a 5% discount rate and a long-term gold price of $3,609 per oz., it calculates an after-tax net present value of $927.6 million and a 48% internal rate of return. Água Azul’s mine schedule spans 13 years, including about a decade at the expanded capacity. Estimated all-in sustaining costs are $1,540 per ounce. The assessment is preliminary and includes inferred resources, which are too speculative to support mineral reserves. The property holds 22.8 million indicated tonnes grading 1.27 grams per tonne gold containing 931,920 oz. gold, according to a July 2026 resource. Inferred resources were estimated at 26.4 million tonnes grading 1.29 grams gold for contained metal of 1.1 million oz. gold. The acquisition comes as ValOre advances processing research at Pedra Branca. On Nov. 10, it announced a five-year cooperation agreement with Germany’s federal geoscience institute and mineral resources agency through the government-funded BioPlat research project. Shares of ValOre were halted Tuesday because the deal constitutes a fundamental acquisition under TSX Venture Exchange rules. They closed at 3.5¢ on Monday, valuing the company at C$8.9 million ($6.2 million).

title: US military pause clouds Ecuador’s illegal mining fight
summary: A Pentagon probe raises uncertainty over efforts to combat criminal gangs that have infiltrated Ecuador’s gold supply chain.
body: A Pentagon probe raises uncertainty over efforts to combat criminal gangs that have infiltrated Ecuador’s gold supply chain. Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa meets US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. ( Image courtesy of Hegseth | X. ) Ecuador’s Interior Minister John Reimberg reaffirmed the country’s security partnership with Washington following reports that the Trump administration had suspended joint military operations, raising uncertainty over efforts to combat drug trafficking and illegal mining. Talks last week with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth focused on reviewing operations, determining next steps and identifying Ecuador’s operational needs, Reimberg said in a radio interview Wednesday, Reuters reported. He described the discussions as productive, pointing to an established action plan between the two countries. “Some would like to see these relationships, which have yielded so many positive results, damaged,” Reimberg said. The remarks follow reports Tuesday by The New York Times and The Atlantic that Washington halted joint operations in mid-October. The US Department of Defense reportedly launched an investigation into alleged human rights violations during a Sept. 23 operation by Ecuadorian forces in Manabí province that killed a suspected criminal leader. The reported suspension comes at a critical juncture for Ecuador, which in July elevated illegal mining to a national security threat after concluding that criminal gangs had infiltrated the country’s gold supply chain, turning the sector into a major source of financing for organized crime. Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa and Hegseth discussed expanding technological assistance, port security and border surveillance during last week’s visit. However, no new agreement was signed amid domestic political sensitivities ahead of the Nov. 29 local elections. Noboa announced in March that Ecuador would conduct joint operations with the US and other allies, describing the initiative as “a new phase” in the fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining. While the initiative has garnered public support, Ecuadorians voted last year against allowing foreign military bases on national territory. Ecuador’s 2026–2029 National Security Plan identifies illegal mining as a strategic security challenge rather than simply an environmental or regulatory issue. The government says criminal organizations use illicit gold production to launder drug trafficking proceeds while supplying mining operations with machinery, chemicals and armed protection. The strategy reflects growing concern over the profitability of illicit gold production, which is fuelling violence and environmental destruction while exposing vulnerabilities in Ecuador’s mineral supply chain. The plan identifies Los Lobos as the country’s dominant criminal organization in illegal mining. A report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) similarly concludes that the gang operates across the gold value chain, from extraction to exports through the ports of Guayaquil and Puerto Bolívar. The Trump administration’s push to expand military co-operation under its American Coalition Against the Cartels faces political obstacles elsewhere in Latin America, where governments must balance security priorities with concerns over sovereignty and the legacy of US military interventions. Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike
summary: Alan Greenspan famously held the line on interest rates because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet boom. Why can't Kevin Warsh do the same?
body: In a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era? Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution. It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation , the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy. Bottom line: the Fed looks like it has to hike — and maybe substantially — to be anywhere close to the position where the Fed was in Greenspan's time at the dawn of a major technological revolution. It may be that the massive capex spending on AI will mean more productivity and less inflation down the road. But the front-end build-out is proving to be more inflationary, and more challenging, to a Fed already dealing with high inflation. In many ways, that's the opposite of what Greenspan had to handle.

title: Crude Oil Price Forecast: Rising Supplies Threaten a Sustained Rally - FXEmpire
body: The latest U.S. petroleum balance shows a near-term counterweight to the tighter global narrative. Commercial crude stocks increased in the week ending November 13. The Energy Information Administrationâs report , released November 18, put commercial inventories at 417.8 million barrels, up 3.4 million from the prior week and 6.4 million below the same week a year earlier. The rise followed a prior draw and leaves stocks close to year-ago levels rather than signaling a severe domestic shortage. Supply remained abundant. EIA estimated U.S. crude production at 14.03 million barrels per day for the week, a 19,000-barrel-per-day increase from the previous week. The 4-week average was 14.01 million barrels per day, 1.9% above the comparable period a year earlier. That production level gives the domestic market a substantial buffer unless refinery demand, exports, or an outage absorbs more barrels. Stable to rising output could replenish stocks when global balances are tight. The interpretation for WTI is less about a single weekly build and more about the direction of the domestic balance. The 3.4 million-barrel build is large enough to challenge a bullish inventory story, but one weekly observation can be influenced by shipping, timing, imports, exports, and refinery runs. Commercial crude is the relevant measure for immediate refinery market availability. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve declined 3.2 million barrels to 276.4 million during the same week. My view at the moment is that WTIâs immediate fundamental balance is somewhat mixed, with the domestic inventory build and high production limiting upside unless the next release shows a reversal. The bearish reading weakens if inventories draw while refinery activity or exports absorb supply. A fresh disruption, weather-related production loss, or sustained pickup in product demand could challenge the comfortable supply narrative. Looking at the chart, it does seem as if the light sweet crude oil market is trying to find some type of floor near the $80 level. As we have dipped towards that area and then bounced again, ultimately this short-term rally opens up the possibility for short-term traders to get involved. title: JP Morgan Outlines Oil Outlook for 2027, 2028 - Rigzone
body: In a new report sent to Rigzone by Natasha Kaneva, J.P. Morgan’s Head of Global Commodities Strategy, analysts at the company, including Kaneva, outlined J.P. Morgan’s oil outlook for 2027 and 2028. The J.P. Morgan analysts revealed in the report that their outlook assumes the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts continue, “yet oil keeps moving and the global market remains in surplus”. “If 2022 and 2026 have taught us anything, it is that wars can disrupt oil flows without stopping them,” the analysts said in the report. “We are therefore modeling a world in which two wars continue, but oil keeps moving,” they added. The analysts highlighted in the report that, “with crude flowing and demand contracting, the global oil market returned to surplus in September”. They pointed out that this excess widened in October and that China has already begun rebuilding its crude inventories, “adding 400,000 barrels per day in October” with the country “on pace to add another 500,000 barrels per day in November”. “We expect that surplus to persist into 2027,” the analysts revealed. “Our forecast assumes Middle Eastern oil flows remain near 90 percent of pre-war levels through March, rising to 94 percent by June and 98 percent by year-end, while demand returns sustainably to pre-war volumes by August,” they added. “China is expected to rebuild crude inventories at an average pace of nearly 700,000 barrels per day, with OECD countries adding another 400,000 barrels per day,” they projected. They warned, however, that, even after accounting for this stock-building, they project a global surplus of 1.6 million barrels per day, “consistent with a Brent price in the high $70s in the first half of the year and the high $60s in the second”. The analysts went on to warn that this surplus will not disappear in 2028. “Even assuming China accelerates inventory accumulation to 1.1 million barrels per day and OECD countries continue adding 0.4 million barrels per day, we expect the market to remain oversupplied by roughly 1.4 million barrels per day, implying a Brent price in the mid-$60s,” they said. “That is our fundamentally driven price forecast, not necessarily the price at which oil will trade throughout the year,” the analysts highlighted, noting that further escalations “could inject substantial geopolitical risk premia into the market”. The J.P. Morgan analysts revealed in the report that they are reluctant to forecast those premia, “let alone embed them permanently into our price outlook”. “History suggests they can be large, but rarely last,” they pointed out. “Since 2005, monthly Brent prices have never exceeded our estimated fair value by more than $24 per barrel, with such deviations lasting an average of just 3.8 months,” they said. “Two wars may keep oil prices volatile. But unless they materially alter the physical balance, the underlying surplus should ultimately prevail,” they projected. The J.P. Morgan analysts highlighted in the report that a “flood of supply is coming”, pointing out that global liquids production “is projected to surge by nearly eight million barrels per day in 2027, reaching 109 million barrels per day, before climbing to 110 million barrels per day by year-end and remaining near that level in 2028”. In their report, the analysts outlined that the U.S.-Iran conflict “has acted like a dam, holding back Middle Eastern production for months”. “Once the barriers are lifted, the rush to reclaim lost market share could unleash a flood of additional supply, particularly from producers outside Iran,” they projected. “By March 2027, we expect Middle Eastern supply outside of Iran to have fully recovered to its 2025 average, before rising further,” they said. title: November 2026: Oil market sentiment shifts back towards oversupply - PetrolPrices
body: At the start of 2026, market sentiment was firmly bearish, with expectations of a global supply surplus and many analysts forecasting that Brent crude would remain below $60/bbl throughout the year. The US and Israeli strikes on Iran, followed by the wider conflict in the Middle East, fundamentally changed that outlook, pushing crude prices above $113/bbl. However, as the conflict has progressed and supply flows have begun to recover, market sentiment is once again shifting towards oversupply. OPEC+ production reached 41.23 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, bringing output close to pre-conflict levels. This recovery in supply, combined with expectations of weaker demand, has increasingly weighed on crude markets. The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects the market to move into surplus as early as the current quarter, while Goldman Sachs forecasts that supply could exceed demand by approximately 2 million bpd as consumption weakens and Middle Eastern flows continue to improve. The shift in sentiment is also evident in investor positioning. ICE Commitment of Traders data showed that, in the week ending 17 November, speculators reduced their net bullish positions in Brent crude by almost 3.5%, taking them to their lowest level in more than ten months. Short positions have also increased, with volumes exceeding 142 million barrels, their highest level in four months. Meanwhile, major investment banks, including Morgan Stanley and JP Morgan, have highlighted the recent build-up in oil inventories as further evidence of a market moving towards surplus. Brent crude has fallen below $87/bbl, down more than 23% from $113.35/bbl at the end of October. The decline in crude has fed through into refined product markets, with wholesale diesel prices almost 20ppl lower than at the start of November and unleaded more than 16ppl lower. Some of these reductions have now reached the forecourt. The average UK unleaded price is almost 12ppl lower than at the beginning of the month. Diesel has fallen more slowly, with the national average currently just under 7ppl lower. The difference in the rate of reduction reflects the pricing dynamics seen during the earlier period of high prices. Retailers were reluctant to push diesel prices above £2 per litre, leaving retail-to-wholesale margins under pressure. As wholesale prices subsequently fell, these margins returned towards more normal levels, delaying the full pass-through of lower costs to motorists. However, the retail-to-wholesale spread for both grades is now above recent averages, suggesting there is further scope for pump prices to fall as we move into December. The pace of retail reductions has also accelerated throughout November, with the number of price cuts increasing each week. Whether this momentum can be sustained into the final month of the year remains uncertain. A continued decline in wholesale costs should support further reductions, although retailers may become more cautious if the rate of wholesale price falls begins to slow. The easing of fuel prices will be welcome news for motorists, retailers and businesses, as well as the government. Lower energy costs should help to moderate inflationary pressures, although the wider impact will depend on how long the decline in wholesale markets is sustained. One factor working against UK fuel buyers is the weakness of sterling against the US dollar. The GBP/USD exchange rate closed at 1.3018 on 23 November, its lowest level since 2 April 2025. Expectations of further US interest rate increases have supported the dollar, while ongoing geopolitical uncertainty has also encouraged demand for the US currency. A weaker pound increases the sterling cost of imported crude and refined products, partially offsetting the benefit of lower international prices. title: Crude Oil Prices Today: Brent Slips Near $91 on Glut Fears - Univest
body: Brent $90.97, down 0.5% (0137 GMT, 25 Nov). Three-month low near $88.40 earlier this week. MCX crude Dec Rs 7,507, down 0.98%. IOC up 1.14%. IndiGo up 1.96%. Crude oil prices eased on 25 November 2026, with Brent crude falling 0.5% to $90.97 a barrel in early Asian trade, after rising more than 2% on Tuesday. Earlier this week, Brent touched a three-month low near $88.40 as worries about a global supply glut outweighed tensions in the Middle East. On MCX, December crude oil futures fell 0.98% to Rs 7,507 per barrel. Lower oil prices helped Indian oil marketing companies and airlines, with IOC up 1.14% and IndiGo up 1.96%. Crude oil prices slipped again on Wednesday as traders weighed signs of ample global supply against ongoing risks in the Middle East. Brent crude futures fell 0.5% to $90.97 a barrel by 0137 GMT, giving back part of Tuesday's gain of more than 2%. The move keeps oil close to the lowest levels in three months. On Monday and Tuesday, Brent dropped to a three-month low in the range of about $88.40 to $88.71 a barrel before recovering. Some trackers showed Brent down as much as 1.2% to around $90.30 later in the Asian session. 5 Hot Crude Oil Stocks in the Buying Zone – Get Them for FREE The swings show how unsettled crude oil prices are right now. A drop to a three-month low, a 2% bounce and then a fresh dip all came within three sessions, as traders react to each new headline on supply and geopolitics. The main pressure on crude oil prices is the outlook for a large surplus. In its monthly report released on 13 November, the International Energy Agency said global supply is set to run well ahead of demand in the fourth quarter. This supply glut concern has kept a lid on prices even when geopolitical risks flare up. Supply is also weighing on crude oil prices from another side. Production from OPEC+ members and from countries outside the group, including the US, has been rising. More barrels coming to market at a time of moderate demand growth adds to the expected surplus. Attacks in the Gulf region have pushed prices up from time to time, including Tuesday's bounce. But analysts say these spikes have faded quickly because actual supply has not been disrupted. Analysts, including Suvro Sarkar of DBS Bank and Tsuyoshi Ueno of NLI Research Institute, have said the oversupply outlook continues to weigh on the market even as geopolitical risks linger. The sharp sell-off in Asian equities on Wednesday, led by chip stocks in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan, also weighed on risk assets, including commodities. When investors turn cautious, oil tends to lose some of its risk premium. Domestic crude oil prices followed Brent lower. On the market, MCX crude oil December futures fell 0.98% to Rs 7,507 per barrel, tracking the weakness in Brent. The Indian contract also reflects the rupee, which has firmed in recent sessions on strong foreign inflows. A stronger rupee lowers the rupee price of imported oil and adds to the downward pressure on MCX crude. India imports most of the oil it uses, so lower crude oil prices are generally positive for the economy. They reduce the import bill , help keep inflation in check and support the rupee. Several sectors benefit directly. Oil marketing companies such as IOC and HPCL buy crude to refine and sell as petrol and diesel. When crude oil prices fall while pump prices stay unchanged, their marketing margins improve, which is why their shares rose on Wednesday. Airlines are another big winner. Jet fuel is the largest cost for carriers such as IndiGo, so lower oil prices feed directly into lower fuel costs and better profits. IndiGo rose 1.96% to Rs 5,631.30. Paint, tyre and chemical companies, which use oil-based raw materials, also tend to benefit. On the other side, upstream producers such as ONGC and Oil India earn less when oil prices fall, so their shares usually come under pressure in a falling oil market. title: Oil prices rise after Houthis say they attacked Saudi refinery - CNBC
body: Crude oil prices rose on Wednesday after Yemen's Houthis said they had attacked Saudi ‌Arabia's largest oil refinery and traders weighed Middle East supply disruptions against the prospect of a global market surplus. Brent crude futures rose 3.5% to close at $94.61 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures climbed 2% to settle at $83.68. Both benchmarks gained more ​than 2% on Tuesday. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Wednesday that they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and ​Riyadh's financial district. The refinery, Saudi Arabia's largest, is part of a complex that also serves as ⁠a major export terminal for Saudi crude. The Houthi statement triggered Wednesday's price rally, said PVM oil analyst Tamas Varga, citing a ​rising geopolitical risk premium. Traders are also likely to be covering short positions ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday, which could add ​to the momentum, Varga said. U.S. crude inventories rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, data from Energy Information Administration showed. That compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a 1.5 million-barrel rise. The build in crude stocks ​was mainly due to weaker crude exports while imports rose, said Bob Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho. Prices also drew ​support from uncertainty about OPEC's 2027 policies ahead of its November 29 meeting, especially with the United Arab Emirates no longer restricted by OPEC+ policies ‌and Iraq ⁠seeking higher oil output capacity, said Zhenqiang Seto, an oil research specialist at LSEG. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide on their 2027 output policy. "Since the release of an IEA report this month, perceptions of a global supply glut have kept prices in check," said Tsuyoshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute. Attention is also focused on how next ​year's production quotas will be ​determined at the OPEC+ meeting, ⁠Ueno added. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said OPEC+ is set to complete a review by year end of member production capacities. Iraq and Kazakhstan were pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate of their oil ​production capacity, said four people familiar with the matter, heightening tensions over a review that ​will help determine ⁠how much members can pump next year. In other supply news, Libya's Sharara oil pipeline has reopened. Flows were halted when a valve was closed by what the National Oil Corporation described as an unlawful group. Oil is again flowing into storage tanks at the Akakus facility ⁠in Zawiya, ​NOC said. In the Strait of Hormuz, a container ship was targeted and came to a ​stop on Tuesday while sailing an "unauthorised" route near the strait, Iran's Revolutionary Guards told state media.

body: WTI crude oil extended its decline to a new low of $80.21 on Tuesday before finding support and advancing to a high of $82.81, at the time of writing. The new low tested a relatively minor potential support area near a prior swing low. Since the trendline is rising, it represents a potential support area that could limit further downside from here. Whether that support holds will be important in determining whether the current decline is nearing an end. There is also a potential falling bullish wedge pattern that has formed during the current decline. A break below the lower boundary of the formation occurred during Mondayâs session and extended on Tuesday. But it looks like a quick recovery of that boundary shows increasing demand. If crude oil can close above that lower boundary line, it would suggest a potential recovery from oversdold conditions that could lead to further strengthening. However, keep in mind that the wedge pattern does not confirm until there is a breakout above the upper falling boundary. Until then, it is only a potential bullish pattern. A quick recovery above the lower boundary would nevertheless add to the significance of support at the $80.21 low. A decline below that low would invalidate the wedge pattern. A decisive rally above Tuesdayâs high of $82.81 would trigger a one-day reversal and increase the likelihood of a counter-trend rally. body: LONDON, Nov 24 (Reuters) – Oil prices fell to three-month lows on Tuesday on signs of rising crude supply and a potential market surplus, though risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz persisted. Brent crude futures were down 75 cents, or 0.8%, at $88.62 a barrel by 0915 GMT, ​after hitting its lowest since August 27. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were 64 cents, ‌or 0.8%, lower at $79.53 a barrel, after falling to the weakest since August 10. “Oil prices are facing modest downward pressure from two sides: markets are pricing out some near-term geopolitical risk in the Middle East, while releases from strategic reserves are keeping supply relatively comfortable despite lower regional exports and stronger Chinese demand,” said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo. “Brent has largely lost any upward impetus in ‌recent ​days as supply conditions remain benign despite the continued closure of the ⁠Strait of Hormuz, and the market ⁠weighs the possibility of a future supply glut against persistent Middle East tensions and shipping disruptions.” However, Suvro Sarkar, head of energy research at DBS Bank, said prices risk going higher again depending on talks between the US and Iran and as both parties could test the other’s resolve in blockading the strait. Iran’s ​Revolutionary Guards navy said three “violating” oil tankers had caught fire after hitting naval mines in the strait on Monday, Iran’s Press TV reported. The United States is also investigating whether Iran was involved in cyberattacks on as ⁠many as 50 energy tankers, the Wall Street Journal reported, ⁠citing US officials and others familiar with the matter. Libya’s Sharara oil pipeline has reopened ​after an “unlawful group” closed a valve on the pipeline, and oil has begun to flow into storage tanks at ​the Akakus facility in Zawiya, the chairperson of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on ‌Monday. China and India are on track for record Russian oil imports this year, plugging a supply gap shortage caused by the Iran war, according to tanker data and industry sources. Temporary US waivers on Russian oil sanctions, aimed at keeping markets supplied amid the Middle East crisis, widened the pool of vessels and suppliers available to India ⁠and China, allowing them to increase purchases. While better supply is weighing on prices, analysts said the market remained fragile. “Oil prices, time spreads, refining margins and investor positioning increasingly suggest the market expects conditions to normalise,” Daniel Hynes, senior ⁠commodity strategist at ANZ, said in a ‌client note. “Yet logistics remain constrained and inventory buffers are thin.” Deutsche Bank said that ⁠global observed liquids’ inventory rose in October, implying an oversupply of 1.7 million ​barrels each ‌day. Evidence is accumulating that the global market is rebalancing and turning ​into surplus, although ⁠setbacks could delay progress, the bank said in a research report. US crude oil and product inventories likely rose last week, a preliminary Reuters poll showed. Elsewhere, Iraq’s prime minister has ordered the federal oil ministry to manage oilfields in areas under Kurdish security control, the state news agency said on Tuesday, potentially deepening tensions between Baghdad and the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region. (Reporting by Stephanie Kelly in London, Vedika Thorat in Bengaluru and Emily Chow in Singapore; Editing by DJ Yap, ​John Mair and Susan Fenton)

title: Oil turns higher as Hormuz disruption fears outweigh improving supply outlook - Investing.com
[MARKET ANALYSIS] Oil futures slightly eased back after yesterday's rebound, while gold is contained ahead of PCE data - Newsquawk
body: Sessions framed around the Strait of Hormuz sit in a well-worn category: the waterway carries a large share of seaborne crude, and episodes of reported closure orders, mine strikes and tanker incidents have historically priced a geopolitical risk premium into prompt spreads and freight and insurance costs faster than into outright flat price, with the premium decaying quickly once physical flows prove uninterrupted. The tell in past episodes of this kind is whether disruption is confirmed in loadings and shipping fixtures rather than in headlines, since rhetoric alone has tended to fade within sessions. Inventory prints from the private survey have rarely sustained direction against a geopolitical driver and mainly set up positioning for the official data that follows. The divergence in the complex is familiar: crude bid on supply-risk, gold sidelined ahead of the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, copper tracking broader risk sentiment, which separates the supply-shock leg from the macro leg. Worth watching are confirmation or denial of the closure order, tanker traffic and insurance rates through the strait, and the PCE release as the next scheduled catalyst for the metals side.

title: Russia’s Elevated Crude Shipments Stoke Global Supply Surplus - Bloomberg
Russian oil exports are pushing the global market toward a surplus - media - Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
body: Russian oil exports reached their highest level since 2022 this year. Analysts expect a global surplus and a possible drop in prices. The increase in oil supplies from Russia is contributing to the formation of a surplus of supply, which is expected to shape the state of the oil market next year and possibly in the years to come. Bloomberg reports, UNN writes. Russia’s exports have averaged 3.65 million barrels per day since the beginning of the year, the highest annual average since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. At the same time, according to tanker-shipment data compiled by Bloomberg, overseas supplies in the four weeks through November 22 fell slightly to 3.92 million barrels per day, 30,000 barrels per day below the revised figure for the period through November 15. The increase in exports adds to growing supplies from the Persian Gulf, prompting an increasing number of market analysts, including Goldman Sachs Group Inc., JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Sanford C Bernstein, to forecast a return to a global oil surplus, which could potentially lead to lower prices. The price of Brent crude has fallen by almost a quarter from its late-October high. On Sunday, oil ministers of OPEC+ countries, led by Russia and Saudi Arabia, are due to hold talks to establish preliminary production targets for 2027. These levels will be calculated on the basis of new baselines, using external assessments of each country’s sustainable production capacity. Russia’s exports have increased this year despite the country’s difficulties in raising production in line with the increase in OPEC+ targets. Strikes on refineries are forcing Moscow to redirect oil it cannot process to exports, increasing overseas oil sales. A lull in these strikes generally allows repair work to be carried out, increasing refining and returning oil to domestic refineries, the publication writes. Russia boosted oil exports to their highest level since July amid refinery strikes - Bloomberg 17.11.26, 16:47 • 7564 views According to Bloomberg, as of November 24, Ukraine had struck 15 Russian oil refineries since the beginning of November. According to Bloomberg’s calculations and government data, the combined design capacity of these refineries exceeds 3.6 million barrels per day — more than half of the country’s total capacity. Two more refineries were hit subsequently. Samara double strike: General Staff confirms the targeting of the Kuibyshev and Syzran oil refineries 25.11.26, 12:56 • 11893 views In the week through November 22, approximately 35 tankers loaded 26.17 million barrels of Russian oil, according to vessel-tracking data. By comparison, 31 million barrels were loaded on 40 vessels the previous week. Supply volumes last week fell by 700,000 barrels per day, averaging 3.74 million barrels per day, offsetting most of the increase recorded the previous week. Weekly supply volumes can be volatile, affected by weather, maintenance, sanctions, military activity and departure times. Data for recent weeks may be revised because a significant number of vessels carrying Russian oil conceal their movements. title: Oil Prices Fall to Three-Month Lows as Supply Outlook Eases, Treasury Yields Ease - Tekedia
body: Oil prices fell to their lowest levels in nearly three months on Tuesday as improving supply prospects, rising global inventories and expectations of a potential market surplus outweighed concerns about continued disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures declined 0.2% to $89.17 a barrel by 1107 GMT, after touching their lowest level since August 27. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell 0.3% to $79.95, having earlier reached its weakest level since August 10. The retreat suggests that oil markets are beginning to price in a recovery in global supply despite the continuing conflict involving Iran and the disruption to one of the world’s most important energy shipping routes. Increased availability of Russian crude, the release of strategic petroleum reserves, and rising global inventories are helping to offset some of the supply losses associated with the Middle East crisis. However, the decline also exposes a growing divide between financial market expectations and the physical realities of oil distribution. While futures prices suggest that traders are anticipating more comfortable supply conditions, shipping disruptions, geopolitical tensions, and limited inventory buffers leave the market vulnerable to another supply shock. “Oil prices are facing modest downward pressure from two sides: markets are pricing out some near-term geopolitical risk in the Middle East, while releases from strategic reserves are keeping supply relatively comfortable despite lower regional exports and stronger Chinese demand,” UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said. Brent has struggled to regain upward momentum in recent sessions as traders weigh the possibility of a future supply glut against continued uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. The waterway is a strategic passageway because it handles a substantial share of global seaborne oil shipments. Prolonged disruption could restrict supplies from major Gulf producers, forcing importers to seek alternative sources and increasing transportation costs. However, a major factor weighing on crude prices is the growing availability of Russian oil to Asian buyers. China and India are on course to import record volumes of Russian crude this year, according to tanker data and industry sources, helping compensate for supply disruptions associated with the Iran war. Temporary waivers issued by the United States on Russian oil sanctions have also expanded the number of vessels and suppliers available to Asian refiners. This has allowed India and China to increase purchases at a time when traditional Middle Eastern supply routes face significant disruption. The development illustrates how geopolitical disruptions can reshape global energy trade rather than simply reduce the amount of oil available. Russian producers have gained an opportunity to redirect supplies towards major Asian consumers, while refiners have diversified their purchasing options to reduce exposure to the Middle East crisis. Strategic petroleum reserve releases are providing another source of supply. By placing additional crude into the market, governments are helping reduce the immediate impact of lower regional exports and limiting the urgency for buyers to compete aggressively for available cargoes. Libya has also restored production flows through its Sharara oil pipeline after an unlawful group shut a valve, according to the chairman of the National Oil Corporation. Oil has begun flowing into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya, adding another source of supply to the market. These developments are bolstering expectations that the initial supply shock could become less severe if alternative producers maintain output and disrupted trade routes gradually reopen. title: Russia Oil Export News: Russia’s Oil Exports Hit 3.65 Million Barrels Per Day, Highest Since 2022 Invasion | Here’s What It Means for Global Oil Prices - The Sunday Guardian
body: Russia Oil Export News: Russia’s oil exports have surged to their highest levels since the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, adding to concerns about a growing global oil surplus and its potential impact on crude prices. Analysts say the rise in Russian shipments, alongside increasing supplies from other major producers, is reshaping the global energy market and could put further pressure on oil prices in the months ahead. According to Bloomberg’s tanker-tracking data, Russia’s oil exports have averaged 3.65 million barrels per day since the start of 2026, the highest annual average recorded since the Ukraine war began in 2022. In the four weeks leading up to November 22, Russia’s overseas shipments stood at 3.92 million barrels per day, highlighting the country’s continued presence in global energy markets despite ongoing sanctions and geopolitical tensions. Experts believe repeated Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have contributed to rising exports. Reports indicate that Ukraine struck 15 Russian oil refineries during November, affecting facilities with a combined processing capacity of more than 3.6 million barrels per day. With refining operations disrupted, more crude oil has been redirected to international buyers instead of being processed domestically. Russia’s growing exports come as supplies from the Persian Gulf and other oil-producing regions also increase. Several analysts and major financial institutions now expect the market to move into surplus, meaning global supply could exceed demand. The International Energy Agency (IEA) reported that worldwide oil supply rose to 105.4 million barrels per day in October, surpassing demand and signalling a potential oversupply scenario. The expected surplus has already started influencing market sentiment. Reports suggest that Brent crude prices have fallen by nearly 25% from their late-October peak, reflecting concerns that an oversupplied market could lead to lower prices if demand does not increase at the same pace. Analysts are closely monitoring upcoming OPEC+ meetings for clues about future production targets and market-balancing measures. India and China continue to purchase the majority of Russia’s crude exports. Reuters reported that the two countries imported an average of 3.4 million barrels per day of Russian oil through mid-November, accounting for more than 80% of Russia’s total crude exports. These strong trade flows have helped Russia maintain oil revenues despite the challenges posed by sanctions and the ongoing conflict.
