Berg said demand is climbing as enterprises rush to adopt Anthropic’s AI coding agents like Claude Code . Goldman Sachs forecasts that revenue will jump from roughly $52 billion in 2026 to $136 billion in 2027, an increase of more than 161%. Needham’s own model is for growth of 156%. “The history of the world’s never seen growth like this before at this scale,” Berg told Fortune , calling Anthropic the “leader in frontier intelligence.” Berg isn’t alone in his view. On Monday, Wedbush also issued a buy call with a $120 price target. Analysts called the stock in a note to clients “the clearest public way to own frontier AI at the start of a very large adoption curve.” The firm added that “the addressable market is vast, spanning a meaningful share of global knowledge work, and enterprise adoption is still early.” Canaccord Genuity initiated coverage Tuesday with a buy rating and a $135 target, pointing to Anthropic’s potential to become “one of the most important enterprise technology franchises of the AI era.” With all of this bullish commentary, why is the stock falling? The backdrop for AI-linked stocks has soured as investors question how long the trade can really last . Nvidia’s Monday rally, sparked by Jensen Huang’s return as CEO , faded on Tuesday as the Nasdaq Composite closed down nearly 1.5%. “I don’t think that short term volatility is unexpected given what we’ve seen,” Evan Schlossman, a principal at investment firm Neostellar Capital, told Fortune . Some experts predict Anthropic could pan out like Facebook’s 2012 IPO . Shares of the company, now known as Meta , dipped below the $38 offer price on the second day of trading and kept sliding, bottoming at $17.55 in September 2012. That was roughly 54% below the IPO price. The stock didn’t climb back above $38 until the summer of 2013, after the company proved it could make money from mobile ads. Meta is now one of the world’s largest companies by market value. “[Meta] stumbled their first quarter out of the gate, and then they got their revenue on their advertising model right,” Berg said. “We saw growth at massive scale for several years in stock, which underperformed and traded below its IPO price then went on to a massive three to four year run.” Not everyone on Wall Street says to buy Anthropic. Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management, warned investors against jumping in, arguing that too much about the company remains unknown . The math behind the buildout worries him most. He cited a Financial Times column last week estimating that Anthropic would need over $600 billion in annual revenue to earn an adequate return on its nearly $1 trillion in infrastructure commitments . That is about seven times its current run rate. title: Nvidia Gets Three Analyst Upgrades After Jensen Huang’s Return: Here’s Why CRWD, LI, DKNG, AMBA Made The List - Stocktwits
body: Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) quickly won back Wall Street bulls after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, while CrowdStrike (CRWD) received two ‘Buy’ upgrades this week. Ambarella (AMBA), DraftKings (DKNG) and Insmed (INSM) drew downgrades, and Li Auto (LI) got a rare, welcome lift from JPMorgan after a third-quarter beat. Eleven days ago, analysts were bracing for the worst. Now, with Huang back as President, CEO and board member, the firms that stepped aside are stepping back in. Bernstein upgraded Nvidia stock to ‘Outperform’ from ‘Market Perform’ and left its price target at $200. The firm had downgraded the stock when Huang's conduct looked likely to cost him his job, and it cut its target in half. The exit came the next day. Huang's departure was the main reason for the downgrade, the analyst said, so his return undoes it. Bernstein still stays positive on the AI buildout. Valuation with Huang at the helm "seems supportive enough to us for now," said the analyst. Oppenheimer's Rick Schafer upgraded the stock to “Outperform” from “Perform” with a $250 target. He called Huang's return a "win for AI and a win for investors" and said it lifts a "major cloud of uncertainty." StoneX went furthest, upgrading to “Buy” from “Hold” with a $270 target. The firm said Huang’s return addresses five issues: the pace of the roadmap, industry relationships, willingness to back the AI buildout, organizational structure and the likely retention of key talent. Guggenheim upgraded CrowdStrike stock to “Buy” from “Neutral” with a $280 target, implying 33% upside. The firm expects "hyper growth and profit." The analyst noted that CrowdStrike works closely with every hyperscaler, even Microsoft, which some investors not long ago saw as a threat to the company's survival. Deutsche Bank's Brad Zelnick also upgraded CRWD to “Buy” from “Hold”, raising his target to $300 from $240. His argument is that the market hasn't fully priced in how much AI will expand the cybersecurity opportunity. He calls CrowdStrike the leader in the space and thinks its $565 billion total addressable market estimate for 2034 will prove conservative given the "tsunami of cyber demand materializing as the AI frontier advances." JPMorgan's Nick Lai upgraded Li Auto to “Neutral” from “Underweight” and nudged his target to $10 from $9. The catalyst was "a clean beat" in Q3, driven mostly by a better product mix and cost efficiency. The firm still expects a cautious industry backdrop into 2027 to weigh on profit. On Wednesday, Li posted its first earnings beat in three quarters . BofA cut Ambarella stock’s rating to “Underperform” from “Neutral” and slashed its target to $30 from $70. Q3 results landed at the low end of guidance, and Q4 outlook came in below consensus. The analyst thinks investors will struggle to underwrite a growth inflection with memory allocation uncertain and AI memory demand strong. DraftKings stock lost an “Overweight” at Morgan Stanley, where Stephen Grambling moved it to “Equal Weight” and lowered his target to $23 from $31. The multiple has compressed and estimates have fallen, he said, because marketing costs are higher again. He argued that visibility and risk-adjusted returns both erode as the company ramps its prediction markets investment. Insmed stock drew two downgrades from Truist and BMO Capital, both tied to Sanofi's (SNY) deal to acquire the company for $175 per share, a roughly $41 billion transaction. title: MU, SNDK, SKHY Jump As Nvidia Tests Kioxia Memory Fix — Analyst Presses Memory Giants For ‘Massive’ Buybacks - TradingView
body: Shares of Micron (MU), SanDisk (SNDK) and SK hynix (SKHY) jumped overnight heading into Thursday after Kioxia said its flash drives could help Nvidia ’s AI chips access a database of up to 2 trillion vectors. For ‘The Nvidia Way’ author Tae Kim, the question is how much confidence memory chipmakers have in their own long-term forecasts. He urged them to show it with “massive stock buybacks.” SNDK led the gains overnight, rising 4%, followed by SKHY up nearly 3%, MU up over 2%, and NVDA up over 1%. In Tokyo, Kioxia Holdings shares climbed nearly 15% to 7,895 yen on Thursday. A day earlier, the company said its operating unit would pay it 2.21 trillion yen on Friday. The cash stays within the Kioxia group. Shareholders will receive a separate payout on Dec. 8, when Kioxia pays its first interim dividend. Nvidia’s (NVDA) GB200 NVL72 rack pairs 72 GPUs with 13.4 terabytes of high-bandwidth memory (HBM). When an AI database exceeds capacity, the system may have to process it in batches and repeatedly move data between storage and memory. Nvidia’s SCADA software lets the GPUs retrieve small blocks of data directly from solid-state drives. For the test, Kioxia equipped one rack with 144 XD8 drives, adding about 1.1 petabytes of raw flash storage, which is 80 times the capacity of the rack’s high-bandwidth memory. Kioxia estimates that the setup could support a database of up to 2 trillion 512-byte vectors, the numerical representations AI systems use to find related information. The companies are still evaluating how efficiently the rack can process data at that scale. “The intelligence of AI agents will increasingly depend on the knowledge they can access, not just the compute power they consume,” said Jason Hardy, Nvidia’s vice president of storage tech. Kioxia also reported results for its next-gen GP2 drive. In a separate test, it handled more than 18 million random reads per second using 512-byte blocks, nearly twice its predecessor’s rate. Kioxia expects to send evaluation samples to select customers by the end of 2027. Kim urged memory chipmakers to back their forecasts by buying their own shares. For Micron, he pointed to Dec. 9. “Otherwise, all the talk about a strong multi-year outlook is just empty words. Show the market through actions,” he said on X. Dec. 9 is when Micron can start using its $35.16 billion buyback authorization under its U.S. CHIPS Act funding agreements. Last month, the board added about $33 billion to the $2.16 billion left under an earlier authorization, based on the company’s quarterly cash flow. Micron can decide how much of that amount to spend. For comparison, it spent $650 million repurchasing 2.5 million shares in all of fiscal 2026. On the other hand, SanDisk spent $5 billion buying back shares in the quarter ended Oct. 2 and still had $10.5 billion available for further purchases. SK hynix, meanwhile, plans to buy back and retire at least 60 trillion won worth of its shares as part of its fiscal 2026 shareholder returns. Data centers are becoming a bigger business for SanDisk , which makes flash memory with Kioxia. In its latest quarter, SanDisk’s data-center revenue rose 61% from the previous quarter to $4.8 billion, while consumer revenue fell 29% to $397 million. The partners are planning for the shift. In August, they outlined plans to invest more than $31 billion in Japan through 2032, contingent on government support. SK hynix could soon become Kioxia’s largest shareholder. It said last week that a bond conversion and share purchase would give it an indirect stake of about 14%. Micron, meanwhile, is already selling drives for AI workloads. In September, it said customers were receiving two lines of SSDs for systems that reuse earlier calculations to speed up AI responses. For investors, the question is how quickly those new uses translate into orders. body: There wasn't all too much in European trading today, with market players bracing themselves for a bit of a break in the second half of the week. The Thanksgiving holiday is upon us and that will see US markets closed today before only opening for more of an abbreviated session tomorrow. As such, thinner liquidity conditions will be a key consideration and that means any modest order flows or sudden headlines could lead to exacerbated price movements in the days ahead. But so far today, we are seeing a calmer mood in broader markets with European stocks catching a strong bounce after the Wall Street turnaround yesterday. Regional indices are holding gains well over 1% in erasing the more negative mood over the past few sessions, and even looking to post a weekly gain now. The DAX is up by 1.8% on the day with the CAC 40 up by 1.6% currently. In the absence of US markets, the dollar is keeping calmer while showing little interest as the recent rally hits the pause button for a moment. EUR/USD is flat at 1.0974 with USD/JPY up by just 0.1% to 159.25 on the day. As for the commodities space, we are seeing oil catch a little bounce with WTI crude up 1% to $84.51 while gold is struggling to build on yesterday's bounce and hold above $3,500 as the precious metal is down 0.3% to $3,571 today. With the Thanksgiving holiday kicking into gear now, I'd be particularly wary of reading too much into any technical breakouts or breakdowns during the coming two days. As much as the turnaround yesterday was quite encouraging, the real test for dip buyers will be whether they can continue to build on that momentum once the usual crowd returns next week. In the meantime, we'll have to deal with a quieter period with potential for some volatility bouts amid thinner liquidity conditions and also month-end flows perhaps. body: Tanker Traffic at Hormuz Ticks Up Despite Intensified Attacks Rystad Energy is an independent energy consulting services and business intelligence provider offering global databases, strategic advisory and research products for energy companies and suppliers,… Norway's transmission system operator Statnett paused new grid reservations for data centers on 9 November, the same day the government announced a licensing scheme that will keep out new crypto mining. The grid reservation halt will last until at least August 2027, when a new system is set to come into effect. Both moves come as data center demand threatens Norway's long-standing power surplus. Data centers have asked for about 34 gigawatts (GW) of grid capacity in Norway, well above national peak demand of about 25 GW. Only 0.8 GW is connected today. Another 4.2 GW holds reserved capacity, 10.8 GW is in the queue, and 18 GW is still at the inquiry stage. Statnett has stopped granting new reservations and approving facility functionality under the Regulation on System Responsibility (fos) § 14 rule while it sets functional requirements for data centers. These will cover when facilities must stay connected during disturbances, how quickly their load may change and how to limit grid fluctuations. Projects with reserved capacity keep their place but still need approval before connecting, and existing connections are not affected. About half of the queue has asked for power by the end of 2028. With no new reservations until August 2027 at the earliest, and grid build-out still to follow, those dates look out of reach for established operators and newcomers alike. Norway is building faster than most of Europe Norway is not alone. Grid operators across Europe are replacing first-come, first-served queues with rules that favor projects able to show progress. Great Britain, Germany and Denmark have all tightened their connection rules since 2025. Satellite images show how far projects due in 2027-28 have to go. In the UK, almost two-thirds of the 2027-28 capacity has no building under way. In the Nordics, it is just over a third. In Norway, about half of the 1.5 GW due in 2027-28 shows new construction, but a single project accounts for most of it. Crypto is on its way out Norway has six operating crypto data centers with about 0.2 GW combined. Under the licensing scheme, new crypto sites will not be permitted, and existing ones cannot get more grid capacity and could face restrictions once transitional arrangements expire. Some operators are already converting to AI. Data center power use in the NO3 price area fell from late 2025 as one large site stopped mining ahead of its conversion, and is now rising again. Pressure on prices Hydro supplies about 90% of Norway's power, and decades of surplus have kept its electricity prices below those in most of Europe. That advantage is set to erode. Under normal hydrology, rising demand from data centers and other consumers could cut Norway's net exports by 71%, from 14.3 terawatt-hours in 2027 to 4.1 TWh in 2030. In a dry year, Norway could become a net importer and winter prices could reach about €290 per megawatt-hour. The government wants the data center industry to help build gas power with carbon capture and storage (CCS) and offshore wind, but both have long lead times. Until new supply arrives, the pause gives Statnett more control over incoming demand and helps limit price risk for households and industry. Between November 1 and 19, the seven-day moving average count showed more than 26 crude oil, fuel, and LNG tankers transiting the Strait each day, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing ship-tracking data by Vortexa. To compare, the seven-day moving average was below 25 vessels on at least two-thirds of the days in October. The vessel numbers come with two caveats. First, the above-mentioned numbers may not be all tankers that have transited or attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz, due to signal interference and en masse switching off of the transponders on the ships. The other is that there has been a slight reduction in the number of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) and Suezmaxes moving through the chokepoint, but the number of smaller tankers, Aframaxes, has increased, according to Vortexa’s data. The change in the tanker fleet operating in and out of the Strait of Hormuz makes it even more difficult for analysts to estimate how much crude oil and fuel are being evacuated from the Persian Gulf and exit the Strait en route to international markets. Smaller oil tankers moved in October the most volumes of crude oil out of the Strait of Hormuz since the war began , as Iran targets supertankers and incidents with naval mines and unknown projectiles hit a wartime high. Moreover, a record number of the so-called long-range-2 (LR2) clean tankers that have transported fuels such as diesel and gasoline have become the so-called dirty tankers and started shipping crude. The LR2 tankers are similar in capacity to the Aframax crude tankers, which can ship up to 800,000 barrels of crude each. A clean-turned-dirty LR2 tanker could be employed on the complex trade shuffles near the Strait of Hormuz, where shuttle-shipments have become the prevailing mode of moving crude oil out of the Persian Gulf in recent months. title: Iranian Hardliners Call for Tanker Convoy to Defy U.S. Blockade
summary: With Iran's revenue from crude oil and condensate exports projected to hit zero by mid-December, hardline commentators and outlets close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) are increasingly advocating a direct challenge to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and waters. body: Tanker Traffic at Hormuz Ticks Up Despite Intensified Attacks RFE/RL journalists report the news in 21 countries where a free press is banned by the government or not fully established. We provide what many… With Iran's revenue from crude oil and condensate exports projected to hit zero by mid-December, hardline commentators and outlets close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) are increasingly advocating a direct challenge to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and waters. Their proposal is for a declared "convoy of tankers" to sail through the blockade, accompanied by threats to target the oil infrastructure of Iran's Gulf neighbors if US forces attack Iranian vessels. Iranian forces already attempted attacks on US targets in Bahrain and Kuwait this week. A campaign promoting the idea of breaking the blockade gathered pace on November 19, when the IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency published a column making the case for a “convoy of oil tankers.” The same day, the ship-tracking service TankerTrackers.com said in a one-line post on X that “Iran appears to be preparing to ship out oil again.” No Iranian official body has formally announced such a plan, but the discussion shows how hard the US blockade is biting. The closest thing to an official signal came from IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi. On November 19, he told a gathering in Tehran, “We will not allow the continued naval, land, and air blockade imposed on our country.” To make its case, the Fars column reached back to the Shahnameh, Iran's national epic. When the mythical hero Fereydun reaches the Arvand River on his way to overthrow the tyrant Zahhak, the guardian of the river refuses him boats. Fereydun does not wait. He and his men ride their horses into the water and cross. “We will not wait for America's permission,” Fars argued. “We open the route and raise the cost of closing it so high that the other side's reason tells it to leave it open.” Fars warned that any attack on an Iranian tanker could prompt Tehran to retaliate against oil facilities across the Persian Gulf, specifically naming those in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. The proposal quickly gained traction among hardline figures, some of whom appeared to present it as an impending decision rather than a suggestion. Lawmaker Ebrahim Azizi, chairman of the parliament’s influential national security and foreign policy committee, declared in English on X that Iran “cannot be blockaded” and ended his post with an hourglass emoji. Hard-line pundit Ruhollah Jomei wrote of “the Islamic republic's decision to load crude oil and dispatch a tanker to China” -- the biggest buyer of Iranian oil. Mojtaba Najafi, whom some Iranian media claim is close to circles of power, wrote, “Apparently, Tehran no longer wants to be a spectator to the blockade and threats.” If the reports are true, Iran is looking to “actively challenge the blockade,” said Hamidreza Azizi, an analyst with the International Crisis Group. Writing on X, he argued that if a tanker gets through, the blockade loses credibility. If US forces stop or strike it, Tehran gains a direct trigger for retaliation. Azizi added that Iran was seeking "to take the military initiative while leaving Washington with the responsibility for triggering the next escalation." According to the energy-intelligence firm Kpler, Iran's revenue from crude oil and condensate exports could fall to zero by mid-December, for the first time in the country's history. The effects of the blockade are already visible in the country's oil shipments. Kpler's data shows that the volume of Iranian oil on the water outside the blockade zone peaked at 88.8 million barrels on July 14, when the blockade was reimposed. By mid-October, that figure had fallen to zero as the last cargoes were discharged in China. Another 43 million barrels remain stranded inside the blockade area, leaving Tehran with a dwindling stockpile of oil that can be delivered to buyers. Speakin

title: Turkey’s Çöpler gold mine restarts after 2024 fatal landslide
summary: Anagold targets 1.3 tonnes of gold by year-end as Ankara pushes to boost domestic production.
body: Anagold targets 1.3 tonnes of gold by year-end as Ankara pushes to boost domestic production. Çöpler sulphide project. ( Image courtesy of Anagold Madencilik. ) The Çöpler mine in eastern Turkey has resumed gold production more than two years after a fatal heap leach failure , restoring a key source of domestic supply in one of the world’s largest bullion markets. Operator Anagold Madencilik began processing stockpiled ore at its pressure oxidation plant in the third quarter under a temporary operating licence, according to Bloomberg . The restart hadn’t previously been announced. Anagold aims to produce about 1.3 tonnes of gold by year-end. Before the suspension, the mine’s annual production stood at about 6.9 tonnes, equivalent to a fifth of Turkey’s total output in 2023. The restart supports Turkey’s ambitions to expand domestic gold production and reduce its dependence on imports. Bullion accounts for more than 60% of the country’s central bank reserves, while the government is targeting annual production of 100 tonnes, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said in parliament this week, without specifying a timeline. The resumption follows the exit of US-based SSR Mining (TSX: SSRM)(ASX: SSR), which sold its 80% stake in the operation to Turkish conglomerate Cengiz Holding for $1.5 billion. Turkey’s Lidya Madencilik Sanayi ve Ticaret AS is a co-owner. The Feb. 13, 2024, heap leach failure dislodged about 10 million cubic metres of material across a 200-metre slope, trapping and killing nine workers. Turkish authorities revoked SSR’s environmental permits days after the disaster and later demanded the company cover cleanup costs. The landslide also raised concerns about potential cyanide contamination of the Euphrates River, which flows through Turkey, Syria and Iraq. Turkey’s environment ministry said water samples showed no signs of pollution, state-run Anadolu Agency reported at the time. The disaster marked the second major operational disruption at Çöpler in less than two years. In June 2022, Turkey’s environment ministry ordered the mine to suspend operations following a cyanide waste spill. Legal proceedings over the fatal landslide remain ongoing. The latest hearing in the trial of 43 people accused of causing multiple deaths and injuries through negligence took place last month, Turkish newspaper Cumhuriyet reported .

title: Congo closes in on Chile’s long-held copper crown
summary: Record African shipments and slowing South American mine output are reshaping global supply.
body: Record African shipments and slowing South American mine output are reshaping global supply. Kamoa-Kakula in DRC is the world's largest new copper mine and Africa’s top copper operation. ( Image courtesy of Ivanhoe Mines. ) The Democratic Republic of Congo is challenging Chile’s dominance as the world’s largest copper producer after quarterly exports surpassed 1 million tonnes for the first time. Congolese copper shipments rose 8% year-on-year to 2.7 million tonnes in the first nine months of 2026, according to government data. Chile exported 1.28 million tonnes in the third quarter, putting the South American nation’s lead within striking distance. High-grade deposits and a wave of investment have more than tripled Congo’s output over the past decade, transforming the Central African nation into the world’s second-largest producer of the metal. Congo’s ascent comes as the world races to secure enough copper to meet rising demand from power grids, electric vehicles and data centres. Chile and Peru, which together account for about a third of global mined output, have struggled to revive growth amid declining ore grades, project delays and permitting challenges. Two large Congolese mines owned by China’s CMOC Group (HKEX: 3993) accounted for almost 550,000 tonnes of exports through September, while Glencore’s (LON: GLEN) operations and the Sicomines complex each contributed 212,000 tonnes. Sicomines is a joint venture between China Railway Group (HKEX: 390; SSE: 601390), Power Construction Corp. of China (SSE: 601669), known as PowerChina, and a Congolese state-owned mining company. Kamoa-Kakula, co-owned by Canada’s Ivanhoe Mines (TSX: IVN) and Zijin Mining Group (HKEX: 2899), exported 187,000 tonnes. The lesser-known Brother Mining Sasu, a joint venture involving China’s Chengtun Mining Group (SSE: 600711), shipped 112,000 tonnes. Chile’s annual output is expected to fall below 5 million tonnes this year, its lowest level since 2003. That would still be about 40% higher than Congo’s 2025 production. The narrowing gap may prove short-lived, however. Chile expects supply to gradually recover as mine expansions and new projects come online, putting the country on track to produce about 6 million tonnes annually by the end of the decade. Congo’s growing clout is also fuelling ambitions to capture more value from its mineral wealth by expanding its role in international commodities trading. State-owned Gécamines, which holds minority stakes in several major mines and has already ventured into copper marketing, plans to establish a trading desk in Switzerland, CEO Baraka Kabemba said Wednesday at the Makutano conferenc e in Kinshasa, Le Point reported. “We cannot be the leading copper producer in the world, be the custodian of the next technological revolution, and not have a presence in the commodities market,” Kabemba said. “From my point of view, that doesn’t make sense.”

title: Chile clears Marimaca to start early copper mine works
summary: The open pit would produce an average of 48,000 tonnes of refined copper cathode a year over its first decade.
body: The open pit would produce an average of 48,000 tonnes of refined copper cathode a year over its first decade. Drilling on the Marimaca project site in Chile. Credit: Marimaca Copper. Chile has cleared Marimaca Copper (TSX: MARI; ASX: MC2) to begin early construction work at its namesake copper project near Antofagasta, two days after a unit of Sprott (TSX, NYSE: SII) backed a proposed financing package for construction. Chile’s National Geology and Mining Service granted the mining-method permit to Marimaca’s subsidiary, Compañía Minera Cielo Azul Limitada. It allows site preparation and bulk earthmoving at the Marimaca Oxide Deposit (MOD) site. Full-scale construction still requires board approval, according to Thursday’s company release . Receipt of the permit “represents another derisking milestone for the MOD project,” BMO Capital Markets mining analyst Rene Cartier said Thursday in a note. “Marimaca is likely to receive additional sectorial permits in due course, though these are not viewed as critical path items.” The permit builds on environmental approval granted in November 2025, “allowing for the commencement of the fully funded early works construction activities at the project,” said José Antonio Merino, Marimaca’s managing director in Chile. The open pit, about 45 km from Antofagasta, would produce an average of 48,000 tonnes of refined copper cathode a year over its first decade. Marimaca put the upfront cost at C$834.7 million ($587 million) and the mine life at 13 years in its 2025 feasibility study. Sprott Resource Lending Corp.’s investment committee backed a proposed funding package of up to $450 million Tuesday. It includes up to $425 million in senior secured debt and up to $25 million in equity under a non-binding term sheet. The first $100 million of the loan would become available after a construction decision, subject to final agreements, due diligence and other conditions, Marimaca said. The oxide deposit has measured and indicated resources of 213.5 million tonnes grading 0.40% copper, containing about 853,800 tonnes of copper, according to an August 2025 estimate. It also holds inferred resources of 21.2 million tonnes at 0.29% copper for about 62,200 tonnes of the metal. The measured and indicated resources include proven and probable reserves of 178.6 million tonnes grading 0.42% copper. Marimaca shares rose 2.4% to C$6.30 Thursday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$854 million ($601 million). The shares have traded between C$5.53 and C$13.49 in the past 52 weeks.

Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos set to lead European Central Bank
summary: De Cos will lead the ECB into a period of political uncertainty and choppy growth, after winning the backing needed to succeed Christine Lagarde next year.
body: Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank next year. He received backing from euro zone leaders at the European Council Summit, multiple media reported on Thursday. The role still requires formal appointment after consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, but neither has veto power and the decision follows intense political wrangling to reach a consensus on who should serve the eight-year term. Reuters reported that de Cos was set for the nomination after the Netherlands agreed to back Klaas Knot, the only other candidate, citing European diplomatic sources. De Cos is a 55-year-old economist and career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and working in various departments before becoming governor from 2018 to June 2024. He chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision from 2019 to 2024, and has been General Manager of the Basel-based Bank for International Settlements since July 2025. Both de Cos and his main rival for the ECB top job, Knot, were widely seen as candidates with deep knowledge and experience in monetary policy and financial stability — attributes that took on particular importance at a time of resurgent inflation, fragmentation and political uncertainty. Lagarde had extensive experience in financial institutions but was criticized by some early in her tenure for a lack of central banking experience. De Cos gained sufficient political backing in closed-door discussions and negotiations since Lagarde said she would step down on Feb. 7, 2027, over seven years after she became the first woman to helm the ECB. That was despite a final push by the Netherlands at the European Council meeting this week backing Knot. Representatives from the euro area's biggest economies — Germany, France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands — have been horse-trading as they look to secure representation on the central bank's six-member Executive Board. Influential roles as chief economist, expected to go to Germany's Markus Brunnermeier, and head of the Markets Portfolio, for which France's Laurence Boone has reportedly been tapped, also change hands in 2027. Analysts say de Cos's commentary and actions over more than two decades at Spain's central bank paint him as moderately dovish — inclined to favor lower interest rates to support economic growth — but also as a pragmatist who has been willing to adapt. That has included support for strong rate hikes during the energy price shock that followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but also giving staunch backing for rates below zero and the huge stimulus package launched by then-ECB President Mario Draghi to reboot the euro zone economy in 2019. De Cos quipped in 2024 that he was an "owl" after being asked if he was a hawk or a dove, emphasizing his focus on data and the situation at hand. "It is true that Hernández de Cos supported the ECB's uber-dovish monetary policy during the period when inflation was persistently below target. However, his monetary policy views may well be regime-dependent," Christian Kopf, head of fixed income and foreign exchange at Union Investment, said in emailed comments. "We are now clearly in a higher-inflation regime, with core inflation in the euro area expected to remain above the ECB's target through 2029." Kopf added that de Cos was the candidate with the "strongest technical understanding of monetary policy and central banking," which he said was important at a time when the world is "witnessing an assault on central bank independence, not only in the United States but also in countries such as Japan." "By appointing a career technocrat such as Hernández de Cos as ECB President, the European Council would send a strong signal that Europe will not waver in its commitment to price stability and that the euro will remain a hard currency," Kopf said. body: Galaxy flags $58,525 as key Bitcoin level after retracting October call Galaxy head of research Alex Thorn retracted his October conclusion that Bitcoin’s bear phase ended in June. He now assesses that the downturn is “very likely” not over, and proposed treating a daily close below $58,525 as a signal for further downside. In the prior report, Thorn relied on a technical signal. In the week ended September 20, Bitcoin moved back above its 50-week moving average, closing at $81,195 versus the indicator at $78,787. Historically, that level has acted as a ceiling during prolonged market corrections. For seven straight weeks Bitcoin held above this line, but in November it fell below it. The week to November 15 closed below the 200-week average. Since 2011, Bitcoin has moved back above the 50-week average 13 times. A new low afterward occurred only twice — in 2021–2022 — and in both cases the price stayed above the indicator for no more than two weeks. Those two failed cases followed more modest declines of 31.4% and 48.2%. In all ten recoveries after drawdowns of 76.7% or more, the prior bottom held. In the current cycle, the cryptocurrency is down 53.1% from its peak. On November 22, Bitcoin closed the week at $61,104 — 17.9% below the 50-week indicator and 10.4% below the 200-week ($68,159). “Its technical argument no longer holds,” Thorn wrote of the October report. From the November 22 level, a rise of roughly 21.8% would be needed to reclaim the 50-week average (around $74,401). Galaxy set December 8 as the deadline for this. According to Thorn, Bitcoin is unlikely to achieve it by that date. He assessed the other three pillars of the October thesis — positioning, fundamentals, and sentiment — as more resilient. Galaxy identified $58,525 — the June 30 daily close — as the primary reference point. On November 22, the price was 4.4% above that mark. Intraday, quotes had already dipped below it: on November 21 — to $55,100. However, the analysts focus on the daily close. Since September, the lowest daily close has been just 0.6% above the June bottom. “We will consider a daily close below $58,525 the start of a move to a materially lower low,” the report says. The analysts cited historical behavior. In seven past cases when the asset broke a low that had held for at least 60 days, the ultimate bottom ended up at least 17% lower. In half of those cases, the drop exceeded 52%. Applied to the June low, that corresponds to roughly $48,500 and $28,200. At the same time, the signals were mixed. November 22 was day 412 since the ATH , whereas prior bear markets lasted from 163 to 406 days from peak to trough. But the drawdown is 53% versus 77%–93% in previous cycles. According to Thorn, by duration the decline should already have ended, but in terms of depth it could still have room to run, and price history alone does not determine which scenario will prevail. Of the 13 bottom indicators tracked by Galaxy, only two had triggered as of November 22. A weekly close back above the 200-week, and then the 50-week, moving average would allow a return to the October scenario, the expert noted. A deepening downturn would be signaled by a weekly close below realized price ($53,205) or a decline in Bitcoin ETP holdings below 1.22 million BTC. Market pressure was compounded by outflows from exchange-traded funds. According to Galaxy, since October 4 U.S. spot Bitcoin ETPs have lost 71,339 BTC ($4.95 billion) — outflows occurred in 22 of 35 sessions. Their holdings fell to 1.24 million BTC — 9.7% below the October 9, 2025 peak. November has already been the worst month for Bitcoin-based ETF s. According to SoSoValue, about $5.39 billion has been withdrawn since the start of the month, even with several trading days left in November. That is more than in any prior month. On November 25, net outflows totaled $453.1 million, extending the streak of negative sessions to seven days. The largest sum — $329.7 million — was pulled from BlackRock’s IBIT.

Galaxy Digital ( NASDAQ: GLXY | GLXY Price Prediction ) has retracted its October 2026 prediction that Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) had reached its bear market bottom. Instead, its research team is now focusing on two lower levels, with the closer one about 20% below the current price. Bitcoin is trading around $60,725, up 3.3% over the last 24 hours, after dipping below the low Galaxy named. So, what levels is Galaxy now considering for Bitcoin’s bottom? Alex Thorn, Galaxy’s head of firmwide research, explained that the October prediction was based on seven consecutive weekly closes above Bitcoin’s 50-week moving average, its average price over the past year. However, Bitcoin closed back below this moving average in the week ending November 8. “The signal it rested on has failed,” Galaxy’s report stated. Following this, Bitcoin fell to $57,208 on November 25, dipping below the $57,700 low from July 1 that Galaxy identified as the bottom. Galaxy examined seven previous instances where Bitcoin broke below a low that had held for at least 60 days. In each case, Bitcoin set a new low at least 17% lower, with the average additional drop around 52%. Applied to Bitcoin’s $58,525 close on June 30, the smallest drop suggests a level around $48,500, while the average drop points to a level near $28,200. The first key level is around 20% below the current price, and the second is about 54% below. Galaxy cautions that history offers no guarantee, and our look at whether Bitcoin drops below $50,000 covers the case for a fall toward the first level. Galaxy CEO Mike Novogratz purchased 411,006 shares of Galaxy stock at $11.73 each on November 20, totaling about $4.8 million, as disclosed in an SEC Form 4 filing. The stock closed at $11.56 on November 25, down 48.3% this year. This purchase suggests that Novogratz sees value in Galaxy’s shares, despite his research team becoming more careful about Bitcoin’s outlook. We think the critical level to watch is a daily close below $58,525, which could signal a move toward $48,500. Currently, Bitcoin is trading about 3.8% above this mark. body: Copper prices staged a notable rebound during Thursday trading, with London Metal Exchange (LME) three-month copper surging as much as 3.4% in early trade to $12,047 per ton before paring some gains. However, analysts at several institutions attribute the rally to position adjustments and a weaker dollar rather than any substantive improvement in supply-demand fundamentals, and say it is still too early to call it a trend reversal. Joe Dickinson, a market specialist at UBS, noted that copper rose in tandem with other base metals, but fundamentals have not changed much, and the move looks more like a technical bear-market bounce than a fundamental inflection point. Since hitting a high of $14,875 per ton in mid-September, copper has fallen about 22% cumulatively, entering technical bear-market territory, and this rebound occurred during a period of thin liquidity ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. Short Covering Drives the Rally, No Sign of Recovery in Demand Market participants widely attribute the rebound to position-level adjustments. Chen Shaojian, co-analyst at Y Capital, said some investors chose to close positions before Thanksgiving and short positions in the metals market had become quite crowded, so this bounce does not necessarily signal a change in the overall trend. In other words, the price increase reflects more passive buying from short covering than a genuine pickup in downstream orders or restocking demand. The weaker dollar also provided some support for dollar-denominated metal prices. But recent U.S. PCE and GDP data came in stronger than expected, prompting markets to reprice the Federal Reserve's rate-cut path, and the scope for further easing remains unclear. Analysts say a sustained rebound in copper prices may require the Federal Reserve to send a clearer easing signal. Precious metals also rebounded from lows in tandem. Laurie Kirby, a foreign exchange and precious metals sales trader at UBS, said the rebound in precious metals from their lows shows there are still funds willing to buy on dips, but stabilization after recent liquidation selling is not enough to confirm a market reversal. Fund flow data corroborates this view: precious metals ETF holdings have fallen only about 1.1% recently, indicating that selling pressure came mainly from futures-market liquidation rather than a large-scale exit by long-term investors. On the physical demand side, the Zurich spot premium has risen, reflecting somewhat stronger physical gold buying; but the options market remains defensive, with the one-month put skew at about 6.5 volatility points, indicating investors have yet to confirm that the worst is over. Unwinding of AI Trades Spills Over into Industrial Metals Pricing The current copper correction is highly synchronized with the cooling of artificial intelligence (AI)-related trades. The 22% decline since the September high broadly matches the pullback in AI concept stocks. Falling GPU rental prices and cracks in the AI circular financing model have further intensified concerns about the sustainability of AI infrastructure investment. Previously, optimistic expectations for AI data center construction and power infrastructure expansion were one of the key pillars supporting copper prices; as related trades cool, investors are beginning to reassess future demand expectations. In its technical report Panorama Económico Departamental, the INEI said Piura was the leading grape-producing department with growth of 448.6%, followed by Lambayeque at 70.4%, Arequipa at 19.2% and La Libertad at 4.4%. The INEI said favorable climatic factors, including rainfall and environmental humidity, promoted the development and filling of pods and helped consolidate flowers and fruit for the export and agro-industrial markets. Ucayali recorded growth of 96.3%, San Martín 3.5% and Huánuco 2.6%; together the three departments represented 64.3% of the national total. Production also increased in Piura at 115.4%, Madre de Dios at 28.8%, Loreto at 10.3%, Amazonas at 2.5%, Cajamarca at 1.7% and Cusco at 1.4%. Declines were registered in Tumbes at 20.2%, Pasco at 1.6% and Junín at 1.2%. San Martín led with growth of 10.7%, followed by Loreto at 6.4%, Lima at 2.4% and Arequipa at 0.9%; together they accounted for 72.3% of the national total. Increases were also reported in Ucayali at 5.7%, Apurímac at 4.7%, Huánuco at 4.6%, Tumbes at 4.0%, Puno at 2.6%, Amazonas at 1.3%, Madre de Dios at 1.2% and Ayacucho at 0.2%. title: Kazakhstan’s inflation forecast for 2026 revised downward to 9.1%, National Bank survey shows - Qazinform
body: The inflation outlook for Kazakhstan has improved slightly, with analysts revising their forecasts downward for 2026 and 2027, according to the latest macroeconomic survey published by the National Bank of Kazakhstan, Qazinform News Agency reports. The survey shows that experts now expect inflation to reach 9.1% in 2026, down from the previous forecast of 9.5%. The projection for 2027 has also been lowered from 8.3% to 8.0%. However, the inflation forecast for 2028 has been revised slightly upward, from 6.9% to 7%. Despite the improved inflation outlook for the coming years, analysts expect monetary policy to remain relatively tight. According to the survey, the base rate is projected to stand at 15.75% by the end of 2026. The median forecast for the base rate in 2027 has been slightly increased from 13.3% to 13.4%, while the projection for 2028 has been revised downward from 11.5% to 10.8%. The survey also covers forecasts for Brent crude oil prices, Kazakhstan’s economic growth, foreign trade and the tenge exchange rate. Experts have raised their average annual Brent crude oil price forecast for 2026 to 93.3 US dollars per barrel. Projections for 2027 and 2028 remain unchanged at 80 and 75 US dollars per barrel, respectively. Meanwhile, Kazakhstan’s economic growth forecast for 2026 has been lowered from 4.8% to 4.6%. The projection for 2027 remains at 4.7%, while the 2028 estimate has increased from 4.4% to 4.5%. A total of 15 organizations participated in the survey, including professional market participants, research institutions, international organizations and rating agencies. The National Bank noted that the survey does not represent its own macroeconomic forecasts. Instead, the published figures reflect the independent assessments and expectations of professional market participants. Earlier, Qazinform reported the IMF forecast faster economic growth in Kazakhstan in 2027.

title: Goldman Sachs Raises Oil Price Forecasts to $105, Citing Middle East Escalation Risks - Vocal
body: Goldman Sachs Group Inc. has significantly raised its oil price forecasts for the end of 2026 and into 2027, citing elevated risks to global supplies amid the protracted and increasingly volatile conflict in the Middle East. In a note released on November 1, analysts including Daan Struyven and Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby projected that Brent crude will reach US$105 a barrel by December , a sharp increase from their previous estimate of US$90. For 2027, they now expect Brent to average US$88 a barrel , a 10% upward revision from prior expectations. The bank also raised its forecasts for the US benchmark, West Texas Intermediate (WTI), aligning its outlook with a broader shift in market sentiment that prioritizes geopolitical risk over fundamental supply data. The revised outlook reflects a market that is increasingly pricing in the possibility of a wider regional war. “Substantial downside supply risks are likely to sustain a large, near-term risk premium,” the analysts wrote. They noted that traders are assigning “increasing weight to escalation after the Nov. 3 US midterms and subsequent potential weakness in Middle East supply.” The timing of this forecast is critical. With the US midterm elections just days away, political uncertainty is amplifying market anxiety. President Donald Trump has repeatedly hinted at the possibility of resuming aggressive military action, including airstrikes against Iranian nuclear and military infrastructure, once the electoral cycle concludes. On the other side, Iran’s Supreme Leader has reportedly ordered top military commanders to prepare for renewed confrontation, signaling that Tehran is ready to retaliate against any perceived aggression. This standoff has created a powder keg scenario where even a minor incident could trigger a disproportionate response, disrupting energy flows from the Persian Gulf. While crude supplies from the Middle East have technically rebounded close to pre-war levels, the fragility of this recovery is a major concern for analysts. Goldman highlighted several potential triggers for further price gains, including intensified attacks on shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint through which about 20% of the world’s oil passes and direct damage to energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, or Iraq. The analysts also pointed to ongoing risks stemming from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which continues to disrupt global energy flows and keep markets on edge. Given the unpredictability of these conflicts, Goldman has adjusted its base case model for 2027 to include an allowance for a one-million-barrel-per-day global supply disruption . This conservative buffer acknowledges that even minor incidents in key chokepoints can have outsized effects on global prices, particularly when spare production capacity among OPEC+ members is already limited. “With the timing and location of disruptions nearly impossible to predict, our base case now includes a one-million-barrel-per-day global supply disruption allowance in 2027,” the report stated. This adjustment suggests that Goldman views the current calm in physical markets as deceptive, masking underlying vulnerabilities that could be exposed at any moment. Goldman Sachs is not alone in its bullish reassessment. ANZ Group Holdings Ltd. similarly increased its year-end outlook for Brent futures to US$105 , warning that the risk of a broader conflict remains "elevated." While analysts previously predicted GDP growth of 4.8 percent, the estimate has now been lowered to 4.6 percent. title: Hormuz Mine Strikes Tie Oil's Surplus Trade to US Naval Staying Power - Crux Investor
body: November's oil sell-off may offer an attractive entry point into non-Gulf crude producers as supply disruptions challenge surplus forecasts. Brent and WTI futures settled at $94.61 and $83.68 per barrel, respectively, after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis claimed strikes on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery and Riyadh's financial district. Iranian state media reported that two tankers struck mines and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz, while the Iranian Army later reported a tanker catching fire after striking a mine, though neither mine-strike report has been independently verified. The rebound follows a nearly 25% decline over three weeks in November driven by supply surplus expectations, while threats to Ras Tanura, a major Saudi export terminal, challenge assumptions of uninterrupted supply. US commercial crude inventories rose 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million but remained 3% below the five-year average, limiting the buffer against further supply disruptions. Gulf crude exports recovered through alternative routes rather than a reopened Strait of Hormuz. Kpler reported that 40% of regional crude bypassed Hormuz through Saudi and UAE pipelines, while most shipments crossing the strait relied on offshore tanker transfers, including those along Oman's coast. Daily Iranian reports of mine strikes and declining Gulf crude flows recorded by Kpler highlight the vulnerability of these arrangements, particularly for exports from Ras Tanura that still require passage through Hormuz. Iran's crude exports fell to 15,806 barrels per day in October under the US blockade, prompting further attacks on commercial shipping. John Kemp, Independent Energy Analyst, noted that October's global oil inventory buildup depended on the US tanker shuttle and blockade, whose high enforcement costs threaten their medium-term viability and the anticipated supply surplus. Daniel Hynes, Senior Commodity Strategist at ANZ, warned that the widening conflict threatens the recovery in Persian Gulf crude exports, which rose last week but continue to decline overall. Despite November's sell-off, the EIA raised its 2027 Brent price forecast for four consecutive months to $85.78 per barrel, even assuming most Middle East oil production outside Iran returns to pre-conflict levels by mid-2027. Chinese independent refiners paid $6 to $9 per barrel above Brent for Iraqi and UAE crude, compressing refining margins when crude costs rise faster than fuel prices. With US refineries operating at 97.5% capacity, limited spare capacity leaves fuel markets vulnerable to further Gulf supply disruptions. Iraq restarted its 120,000-barrel-per-day Kirkuk-Fishkhabour pipeline and is targeting exports of 500,000 barrels per day to Turkey. While Gulf producers must expand alternative export routes, non-Gulf producers selling crude at Brent- or WTI-linked prices can benefit from higher benchmarks without incurring Hormuz-related rerouting costs. The duration of US naval operations and the outcome of OPEC+'s November 29 meeting on 2027 production policy remain uncertain. Brent's nearly 25% decline over three weeks underscores the importance of sizing positions in non-Gulf oil producers to withstand comparable price declines while retaining exposure to a potential recovery. body: Brent crude rose 3.5% to US$94.61 a barrel on 25 November 2026 after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura refinery and Riyadh’s financial district. The prospect of a disruption to Saudi oil supplies lifted prices despite expectations of a global surplus. Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery, is part of a complex that also serves as a major crude export terminal. A person with knowledge of the matter confirmed to Reuters that the refinery had come under attack. The Saudi government and state oil company Aramco did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment. The effect on refinery output and shipments remained unclear. Both crude benchmarks extended gains of more than 2% on 24 November. Prices on 25 November were: - Brent crude settled at US$94.61 a barrel, up US$3.21 or 3.5%. - US West Texas Intermediate crude rose to US$83.68 a barrel, up US$1.63 or 2%. Tamas Varga, an oil analyst at PVM, said the Houthi statement prompted traders to pay more for crude to cover the risk of a supply disruption. Traders who had bet on lower prices were also likely buying back contracts before the US Thanksgiving holiday, Varga said. Phil Flynn, an analyst at Price Futures Group, said Middle East tensions were making investors nervous ahead of the weekend. Near the Strait of Hormuz, a container ship had been targeted and had come to a stop on 24 November while following a route Iran’s Revolutionary Guards described to state media as “unauthorised”, according to the Guards’ account. In Libya, the Sharara oil pipeline reopened after a brief stoppage. The National Oil Corporation said a group it described as acting unlawfully had closed a valve. US commercial crude stocks rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million in the week ending 20 November, according to the US Energy Information Administration. Crude exports fell by about 1.2 million barrels a day to 3.3 million. Analysts polled by Reuters had expected US stocks to rise by 1.5 million barrels. Flynn said the smaller increase gave oil prices a further boost. Ministers from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, known as OPEC+, will hold a series of meetings on 29 November to decide their 2027 output policy. Four people familiar with the matter said Iraq and Kazakhstan were pressing the alliance to raise its estimates of how much oil each could produce. Those estimates will help determine their quotas. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said OPEC+ expected to complete its review of members’ production capacity by the end of 2026. Zhenqiang Seto, an oil research specialist at the London Stock Exchange Group, said Iraq was seeking to expand its capacity while the United Arab Emirates was no longer bound by OPEC+ production limits. Tsuyoshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute, said the prospect of excess supply had limited price gains since the International Energy Agency published its November oil market report. Oil prices fall as supply concerns linger after Iran claims mine strikes on ships - Business Recorder
body: Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, including Houthi attacks and Strait of Hormuz incidents, drove crude oil prices up, overshadowing supply surplus concerns and potential OPEC+ output decisions. LONDON: Crude oil prices rose $1 on Thursday, reversing earlier losses, after Yemen’s Houthis said they hit Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery and Iran said mines struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz, reviving concerns about supply disruption. Brent crude futures were up $1.64, or 1.73%, at $96.25 a barrel by 1425 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose $1.10, or 1.31%, to $84.78. There will be no settlement for WTI on Thursday because of the US Thanksgiving holiday. “The perceived supply surplus in the coming months and quarters and sticky inflation, which forces central banks to raise rates, resulting in a stronger dollar, will possibly set a ceiling on any attempt to push prices significantly higher,” said PVM Oil Associates analyst Tamas Varga. “The new trading range, it appears, is around $88-$97, basis Brent.” Brent settled up 3.5% in the previous session while WTI climbed 2% after Yemen’s Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura oil refinery and Riyadh’s financial district. The refinery, Saudi Arabia’s largest, is part of a complex that also serves as a major export terminal for Saudi crude, and analysts expect the latest reported Houthi attacks to increase oil’s geopolitical risk premium. The Saudi government and state oil company Aramco did not respond immediately to requests for comment. At the same time, shipping has been disrupted through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil supply had been recovering to near levels achieved before the US-Israeli war on Iran. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Thursday that two tankers had exploded and caught fire after hitting sea mines north of Oman’s Khasab port while attempting to cross the strait. One of the vessels was a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, the Guards said. “The broadening of the Middle East conflict threatens to halt the recovery in oil flows,” said ANZ analyst Daniel Hynes. An initial estimate of last week’s Middle East crude exports, including non-Hormuz routes, put them at 15.3 million barrels per day, Morgan Stanley analysts said in a note. OPEC+ ministers will hold meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. They face the challenge of balancing output with the United Arab Emirates no longer in the group, and with Iraq and Kazakhstan pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate of their oil production capacity. Two people with knowledge of the matter said OPEC+ may roll over its current oil output targets at the coming meeting for at least the first quarter of 2027. In the US, crude stocks rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, the Energy Information Administration said. That supported prices because analysts had expected a rise of 1.5 million barrels. Meanwhile, refinery capacity was taking a hit. In Asia, Thailand’s Bangchak Corp said it had shut all production units at its Phra Khanong oil refinery in Bangkok after a fire. A drone attack at the Slavyansk ECO oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region also led to a fire, inflicting serious damage.

title: Oil Prices Rise as Hormuz Attacks Clash With Forecasts of a 2027 Supply Surplus - Blockonomi
body: The oil market is trying to price two stories at once. One says the world faces a large supply glut next year. The other says the world’s most important oil shipping lane is running at around half its normal traffic, under attack, with little backup supply. BREAKING: Oil surges above $85 following Houthi attacks on Middle Eastern infrastructures and maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz. pic.twitter.com/rllB16tE8L The lead story has flipped quickly. On Monday, Brent’s January contract closed at $89.37, its weakest finish since Aug. 28, after three straight weekly losses. By Thursday, Brent was trading at $91.86 in Europe, according to Investing.com , after a new wave of attacks across the Gulf. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said three more ships were struck by projectiles heading east through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s Fars news agency reported that another tanker had hit a naval mine. Houthi militants aimed four drones at Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura refinery and two Red Sea ports. Bahrain reported an Iranian attack on a civilian industrial site, and Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed strikes on U.S. positions there. The International Energy Agency expects supply to exceed demand by 1.7 million barrels a day this quarter, widening to 3.8 million barrels a day in 2027. U.S. crude stocks rose 1.1 million barrels in the week to Nov. 20, the third straight weekly build, the Energy Information Administration reported. Dennis Kissler of BOK Financial wrote in a note on Monday that the attacks have not stopped oil from moving: “Global crude oil exports remain ample… While attacks are still occurring…oil flows are reaching destinations.” He called Iranian claims that more than 35 large tankers hit mines in 20 days “nearly impossible” given current flows. ANZ analysts estimate Hormuz throughput at 49% of normal. They warn that low global inventories and almost no spare production capacity leave the market exposed. UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo has said prices underestimate the combined risk of depleted inventories, recovering Chinese demand and ongoing disruptions. Even the basic numbers don’t line up. Preliminary Kpler data showed Hormuz transits 42% below prewar levels in the week to Nov. 21, which is closer to 58% of normal than ANZ’s 49%. The figures cover different periods and may measure different things. Demand signals are mixed too. Investing.com linked a drop in U.S. crude exports, which fell to their lowest since early August, partly to softer Asian demand. This is not the first time a Gulf shipping war has met a glut. During the Iran-Iraq “Tanker War,” which began in 1984, hundreds of merchant ships were attacked. Yet oil prices collapsed in 1986. Spare capacity was a big reason. Saudi Arabia had cut its output deeply earlier in the decade, leaving it large volumes it could bring back. ANZ says that cushion is missing now. If that is right, today’s glut forecasts depend heavily on one assumption: that Gulf oil keeps getting through the strait. OPEC+ ministers meet Sunday, Nov. 29, to set 2027 output policy, with Iraq pushing for more room to pump. But most Iraqi crude ships from terminals near Basra, inside the Gulf. Safe passage may matter more than higher quotas. Vice President JD Vance met Qatar’s prime minister this week, but U.S. efforts to win nuclear concessions from Iran remain stalled. Tehran has threatened to tighten control of the strait unless Washington lifts its naval blockade, eases sanctions and frees Iranian assets. Thin Thanksgiving trading could exaggerate price swings this week. After that, the next weekly count of Hormuz traffic may tell traders more than any annual forecast.

title: First Trust’s Fed Forecast: Interest Rate Hikes in 2027 May Fall Short of Expectations - Cryptonews.net
body: First Trust economists argued that the market expects the Fed to raise interest rates more than necessary by 2027. The assessment comes at a time when a further increase at the December meeting is strongly priced in. Polymarket’s November 26th outlook shows a 25 basis point rate hike with a probability of approximately 94 percent. However, the main debate among economists centers on how long the tightening will continue after the December decision. At Polymarket, the probability of interest rates remaining unchanged is approximately 3.5%, while the probability of them being increased by at least 50 basis points is 2.1%. Each of the rate cut options remains below 1%. The Fed’s current policy interest rate is in the 3.75–4.00% range. If the expected 25 basis point increase occurs, this range will rise to 4.00–4.25%. These rates reflect the pricing of participants trading on Polymarket. While there is a clear consensus on the number of increases expected throughout next year, the same level of confidence is not reflected in the overall figures. Where First Trust deviates from market expectations is the future trajectory of inflation. Economists noted that the M2 money supply grew by 0.5 percent in October, or 5.9 percent year-on-year. They compared this rate to the average of approximately 6 percent during the 2010s, when inflation mostly remained below 2 percent. According to the report, current money supply growth could create a picture consistent with lower inflation next year. Therefore, economists do not expect all the increases priced for 2027 to materialize. Consumers’ spending capacity also plays a significant role in the assessment. First Trust added that spending is growing faster than income and the savings rate has fallen to 4.1 percent. They believe that low savings support current consumption but make it difficult to sustain spending at the same rate in the long term. Economists are not calling for interest rate cuts due to current inflation. Their objection is based on the view that the Fed will have to tighten more than expected in the market next year. Data released by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis on November 25th shows why the Fed remains cautious. In October, annual PCE inflation was 3.8 percent, and core PCE inflation was 3.3 percent. Both indicators saw a monthly increase of 0.3 percent. Consumer spending increased nominally by 0.3 percent; however, inflation-adjusted spending remained almost unchanged. This presents a picture where real growth in consumption has stagnated while price pressures persist. Such a development is one of the conditions that could reduce the number of additional increases the Fed would need. title: Fed's preferred gauge of inflation climbs ahead of possible rate hike - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
body: The Fed will issue a decision on interest rates early next month. The Federal Reserve's preferred gauge of inflation climbed in October, according to a government report issued on Wednesday. The measure is sure to draw attention from central bankers as they weigh a possible rate increase early next month. The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE) showed annual inflation climbed from 3.6% in September to 3.8% in October. The reading matched economists' expectations. That figure for October marked the highest annual PCE in five months, putting inflation nearly two percentage points above the Fed's target level of 2%. The report arrived weeks after a separate inflation measure, the Consumer Price Index (CPI), showed a larger jump in prices in October than economists had expected. Fuel prices have accounted for a sizable share of overall inflation since the outbreak of the Iran war in late February set off a global oil supply shortage. A cooldown in oil prices since the midterm elections has put downward pressure on gasoline prices, however, leaving the national average price of a gallon of gas at $3.58 as of Wednesday, AAA data showed. That figure amounted to a decline of about 15% from a month earlier. The relief at the pump in recent weeks did not appear in the report on Wednesday, since it detailed prices in October. The fresh data is sure to garner attention from the Fed at a delicate moment, when policymakers are weighing a rate increase that could help tackle inflation but risks a slowdown in hiring. A stronger-than-expected jobs report earlier this month may ease possible concern among central bankers about a cooldown for the labor market. Economic growth has also proven resilient, displaying better-than-expected performance in a quarterly report on gross domestic product released last month. If the Fed were to issue a rate increase at its next meeting in December, the decision would mark the central bank's second rate hike in four months, after it had gone three years without raising rates. The odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting are pegged at about 97%, according to CME Group's FedWatch Tool , a measure of market sentiment. Days before the midterm elections, Fed policymakers opted to hold interest rates steady as they awaited further economic data. Still, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh vowed to cool off inflation. "It’s our responsibility to get inflation down," Warsh said at a press conference in Washington, D.C., at the time. Wall Street will also take notice of the PCE report after a volatile stretch of trading. The major stock indexes were mixed on Tuesday after soaring a day earlier in response to an announcement from Nvidia reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. Those fluctuations followed a selloff last week as tech investors digested fallout from Huang's previous resignation as well as an initial public offering from artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.

body: Nvidia's (NVDA) board voted on Nov. 22 and announced on Nov. 23 that it had unanimously approved restoring Jensen Huang's roles as president, CEO and director, effective immediately. The news sent Nvidia shares soaring 31.48% that day to close at $165.05, adding roughly $952 billion in market value in a single session. The Nasdaq Composite rose 6.51% in tandem, the S&P 500 Index gained 4.73%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index jumped about 14%. But the rally ignited by the personnel decision lasted only one trading day. AI-related shares gave back their gains across the board the next session, and Nvidia closed down 5.86% at $155.38 on Nov. 24, signaling that investors still harbor doubts about variables beyond the leadership question. Bernstein, in a team led by analyst Stacy Rasgon, upgraded Nvidia to "outperform" from "market perform" shortly after the reinstatement was announced, but kept its price target unchanged at $200. Just 11 days earlier, the same team had downgraded the stock citing the possibility of Huang's departure and slashed its target to $200 from $400. Based on the Nov. 20 close of $125.53, the $200 target implied roughly 59% upside; with the stock's sharp rebound, that gap has narrowed considerably. The rating and the price target actually answer two different questions. Under Bernstein's definition, "outperform" means the stock is expected to beat the S&P 500 Index by at least 15 percentage points over the next 12 months; the $200 figure is a price derived from earnings forecasts and valuation multiples. Huang's return removed the main trigger for the earlier downgrade, and the stock's steep slide during the turmoil widened the gap between the market price and the target. title: Nvidia Reportedly Halts AI Chip Shipments To Southeast Asia As U.S. Tightens China Curbs - Forbes Africa
body: Nvidia has instructed its manufacturing partners to halt shipments of servers equipped with its artificial intelligence chips to four Southeast Asian countries, the Financial Times reported Thursday, as the Trump administration moves to restrict Chinese AI companies’ access to advanced American semiconductors amid heightened scrutiny of the chipmaker’s business dealings in the region, following the controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang. Citing three unnamed sources, the FT reported that Nvidia’s manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, have informed customers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that the chipmaking giant will not allow their servers to be shipped. The report notes that it is unclear if the suspension is temporary to allow Nvidia and the server makers to address compliance with new U.S. export control rules. The reported shipment freeze comes a week after new U.S. export restrictions went into effect, requiring companies to obtain licenses to ship advanced AI chips to the four Southeast Asian countries and Brazil, with exemptions for qualifying U.S.-based companies. The move also follows the Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate billionaire Jensen Huang as its CEO and the establishment of an independent National Security and Export Control Committee. Bloomberg separately reported on Wednesday that the new restrictions have prompted lenders to pause billions in financing for Asian data center projects linked to Chinese technology giants, including ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent. Reuters reported on Thursday that China’s Z.AI could delay the launch of its next flagship model, GLM-5.5. The company originally planned to release GLM-5.5 this month and later shifted its target to year-end, but the launch could now slip into the first quarter of 2027. The report also noted that rival Moonshot AI believes its six-month development cycle for models could double to a year or longer if it loses access to Nvidia chips hosted by overseas cloud providers. Its current flagship Kimi K3 model launched in July this year and the restrictions could push back the launch of its successor K4 to mid-2027. The chip restrictions come as the companies also face increased efforts by OpenAI and Anthropic to prevent distillation of their cutting-edge models. Distillation is a process that lets companies train models using outputs from more advanced models at a fraction of the cost. Despite the Commerce Department’s announcement of new export restrictions, Nvidia raised its revenue growth forecast for fiscal 2028 from 70% to around 75% and projected revenue of around $130 billion for the current quarter. During the company’s earnings call , Nvidia CFO and then-interim CEO Colette Kress acknowledged the new export restrictions, but said: “With demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong.” Kress also said the company had assessed the new curbs while preparing its revenue forecast but was still studying their implications. It’s unclear if the projection could be impacted by this reported freeze in shipments. Nvidia’s stock price fell 3.91% on Wednesday, ending the trading day at $149.30. Shares inched up around 1.3% to $151.23 in after-hours trading, but U.S. stock markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. The chipmaker’s shares surged more than 31% to close at $165.05 on Monday after the board announced Huang’s return as CEO. Despite giving up some of those gains over the past two days, Nvidia’s shares remain nearly 19% above Friday’s closing price. Its data center business alone posted quarterly revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% year over year and accounting for more than 90% of total revenue. That strong growth had long earned Nvidia's stock a rich valuation, with its price-to-earnings ratio earlier this year at one point exceeding 40 times—far above what the analyst was willing to pay. DiLallo took the opportunity to establish an initial position and believes there is still a strong chance of double-digit annualized returns over the next five years; if the stock keeps falling and the long-term investment thesis remains intact, he will consider adding more. title: 5-Star Analyst Revamps Nvidia Stock Price Target for 2027 - Yahoo Finance
body: Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives raised his price target on Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) to $250 from $225 following CEO Jensen Huang's return, saying the executive is worth $1 trillion to the company's valuation, according to a CNBC interview. The new target, an analyst's estimate of future share value, implies roughly 60% upside. The $25 increase covers about one-third of the $75 gap to his unchanged $300 bull case, or best-case scenario. He called the CEO's return a watershed moment but did not raise the target to $300, citing ongoing issues, including federal probes into the company. In a post on X, Ives said Huang's return brings stability back to the company. He added that Nvidia remains two to three years ahead of competitors, including those in China. Ives also said Wall Street estimates continue to understate Nvidia's multiyear outlook. U.S. customers seeking Nvidia chips today face delivery dates stretching to the end of 2028, he said.
